The effectiveness of text-generation models can be enhanced through the use of visual support, but integrating images into input texts poses a significant challenge due to the diverse ways images can be described. To address this issue, a new task called describe-for-captions (DFC) has been designed, which involves teaching text-generation models to produce descriptive captions for given images. To determine the impact of images on the generated text, a new metric called image-based coherency has been developed, which shows that images can substantially influence the content of generated texts. Through experiments with various text-generation models, it was found that pre-trained Transformer models can effectively produce descriptive captions for seen and unseen image descriptions without requiring explicit ground truth descriptions.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through a benchmarking analysis to determine its performance characteristics.
Notably, Delegated RingCT is shown to be secure in the random oracle model and enjoys the benefits of being non-interactive while providing anonymity, without sacrificing public key encryption security.
In comparison to other RingCT variations, the Delegated RingCT scheme boasts significantly enhanced transaction processing efficiency, exceeding that of the Basic RingCT scheme by DLRCT, as evidenced by the benchmarking analysis.
Furthermore, the Delegated RingCT scheme is distinguished from DLRCT in its ability to process transactions at an even higher speed, representing an increase of more than 10 times.
Consequently, the Delegated RingCT scheme is suited for practical use in large-scale public blockchains due to both its computational efficiency gain and its increased throughput, which effectively protects the anonymity of transactions.

A new method of using data from the HERA-II hydrogen hydrogen running frame to determine the scintillator system's gain and efficiency is presented. This method involves taking continuous readings of the left and right scintillator groups over a 1-second interval and converting the data into brightness units. The brightness data is used to identify and remove problematic channels. The remaining data is used to calculate an average signal, an overall system gain, and an overall efficiency for each trigger pair. These values can then be used to determine an overall efficiency for the scintillator system and to identify poor-performing channels. The technique has the advantage of being able to identify and remove low-quality data in real time. It also allows for the identification of channels that were working properly during data collection but are not functioning correctly.

Our goal is to develop a predictive model that leverages both supertree features and information from the individual tree level, thereby addressing the limitations of traditional logistic regression models that can be overly optimistic due to limited data availability per tree. To achieve this, we've constructed a graphical model structure that integrates the probabilities of being green, annotated, and labeled, while considering the interdependencies between label probabilities and generating a predictive probability for being green. The proposed model has been successfully applied to a dataset from the Amazon Machine Learning Basin Open Data Initiative, thereby demonstrating improved accuracy and a more nuanced understanding of the data, thereby uncovering patterns and correlations at the tree level. The model and data can be accessed through a public GitHub repository.

Our study examines the potential for the $\Upsilon(10753)$ pentaquark to decay into $\Upsilon(1S)$ or $\Upsilon(2S)$ bottomonium through the emission of two pions. The consideration here is the first observation of a decaying $\Upsilon(10753)$, where it breaks down into the $\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$. The proposed two-diagram model explains the nearly equal branching ratios for the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-)$ and ($\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(4S)\pi^+\pi^-)$ transitions, which were both observed in an experiment. The new results from our study, however, indicate a lower branching ratio for the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-)$ transition, which was previously observed, and also show that the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(4S)\pi^+\pi^-)$ transition has a smaller branching ratio than previously estimated. The study also forecasts potential observability for the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-)$ and ($\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-)$ transitions with the upcoming $\J\psi\Upsilon$ data collected by

This research introduces a novel optimization method, AskewSGD, an iterative approach tailored for training deep neural networks with quantized weights using subgradient calculations. We derive this method by analytically resolving a constrained optimization problem for quantized models, preceding it with a theoretical guarantee of existence for the optimal solution. We also offer a dynamic solution for adapting model parameters to changing quantization limits. AskewSGD outperforms competing methods on both MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, showcasing its efficacy in automated neural architecture design under quantization constraints.

Over the past twenty years, there has been a significant shift in robotics research, with a growing emphasis on soft robotics. This field, which was pioneered by Robotica, has now evolved to resemble a classic actuator-based robot system, with the exception of softer body parts. This transformation is not merely a technical advancement; it also reflects a significant paradigm shift towards a more biologically inspired approach. This new perspective seeks to integrate robotics, biology, and medical expertise to address long-standing research hurdles, thereby paving the way for substantial breakthroughs in fields such as healthcare and environmental science. This work surveys current research in soft robotics and control, with a particular focus on model-based control, systems with multiple flexibility, and the merging of modeling and control frameworks. We also identify and critically evaluate the key challenges hindering the development of soft robotics and propose innovative solutions to these problems.

This note re-examines the Authentic Jacobi Group and establishes that its Schur-Weyl unitary irreducibility criterion can also be proven using the centralizer method, and its centralizer described completely, casting light on a long-standing puzzle from "The Authentic Jacobi Group" paper.

In natural language processing, fact verification involves determining whether a given text represents true or false information. Two primary types of verification data, "table-oriented" and "text-based," present different formats for assertion validation. The former incorporates tables that express facts precisely, whereas the latter involves narrative text requiring fact extraction. The success of deep learning models in processing table data has been impressive, but they often falter when faced with disintegration tasks, which involve separating embedded facts from surrounding context. As disintegration appears crucial for navigating complex fact verification datasets, this study assesses the disintegration capabilities of leading deep learning models for table-oriented fact verification. The findings reveal that these models struggle with disintegration, and their performance improves minimally when given explicit guidance on fact representation. To address this issue, this research introduces a novel rule-based disintegration model specifically designed for table-oriented fact verification. The results indicate that this approach surpasses existing deep learning models in disintegration and also enhances the overall fact verification task performance.

Generative adversarial networks, or GANs, employ an unconventional approach to develop high-quality artificial images and videos that resemble real ones, using an opposing network that trains them through frustration. One of the primary issues with this approach is that the generated content often lacks a clear connection to the input image, which is necessary for creating realistic outputs. A new technique, referred to as hidden space conditioning, has been proposed to overcome this challenge, which involves selecting specific image regions to work with. The goal of this technique is to expand the scope of images that a given model can accurately replicate. In our research, we will draw from existing knowledge on image processing and learn how a GAN model's hidden spaces can be utilized to make informed decisions about content and composition. An in-depth analysis of various hidden spaces, including those governed by human perception, will be presented, accompanied by a systematic evaluation of their capabilities. Ultimately, our findings will demonstrate the feasibility of integrating these principles and revealing the underlying structures of a network's hidden spaces.

In our investigation of a novel method for dynamic analysis of stochastic processes, we focus on a class of algorithms that exploit structural properties of a system to reduce computational complexity, specifically those that can make use of such properties to sample partially. This study evaluates a set of sampling techniques that can take advantage of system properties to reduce the complexity of dynamic analysis, including both deterministic and stochastic methods. It provides a clear definition of the requirements a probability distribution must meet in order to be useful in this context, and identifies algorithms that generate distributions meeting these requirements. The performance of these algorithms is evaluated in two experimental settings, showing that some may significantly outperform others even when the system is relatively small. Notably, none of the tested algorithms consistently performed better than the others in all settings.

This research paper explores the concept of fault-resistant distance labeling on tree graphs, particularly in scenarios where node faults result in edge reconnections. To achieve this, we demonstrate the feasibility of constructing path labeling schemes with optimal length and constant vertex arboricity, and in the process, we contribute a new distance tagging scheme with length O(n^{1/2ε} log^2 n) for planar graphs with vertex arboricity ε. Additionally, our findings for tree graphs show that, with 1 fault tolerated, verifiable distance labeling requires length at least 5.623n, and we establish the validity of this lower bound by constructing a specific tree with the same distance label for any valid path labeling scheme, and demonstrating that any path labeling on this tree can be converted to a verifiable path labeling with a reasonable increase in length.

Researchers explore the dynamics and spectral characteristics of a modified Bose-Hubbard model that incorporates features of non-radiative energy loss and non-conservative dynamics.  This investigation specifically analyzes how changes in non-radiative and non-conservative dynamics impact the overall spectral density and statistical relationships between different modes of the system.  The findings show that both types of non-conservative dynamics produce similar effects on the system's behavior.  The conclusions derived from this study through theoretical analysis, specifically through a mean-field approach, provide insight into the system's relaxation and quasi-resonance phenomena that occur following a sudden introduction of non-conservative dynamics.  The study's results can be verified in experiments involving compound optical or gradient optical micro-machines that contain two-mode, two-eclipse systems.

We're focusing on the second-order elliptic equations in divergence form, applied to static situations within a given bounded domain in n-dimensional space. It's assumed that certain and certain vector fields have square-integrable representations within the domain and that the equation's right-hand side also has its representation as part of $L^2$ in the domain. Our research includes studying a wide variety of elliptic equations, such as general types, degenerate types, and strongly degenerate types. Our main finding is the uniqueness of weak solutions for a broad category of these equations, including both general and degenerate types. Our research is also theoretical and has the advantage of being simplified and refined. Our methods involve representing the equation in question in a specific type of matrix-valued function and establishing that it's related to a specific type of mathematical operator that has properties similar to those of a general elliptic operator. This allows us to make inferences about the equation. Our research extends to and incorporates the study of stationary situations in non-local problems, providing an abstract definition for currents of a specific type and a mathematical operator that can be used to prove a unique weak existence theorem for these equations.

In the realm of Out-of-Sample (OOS) detection, advanced analytical techniques play a crucial role in identifying unusual data patterns that deviate from established trends. A renowned method within this area is the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test, though it exhibits limited capability in detecting intricate, non-Gaussian data anomalies. On the other hand, Bayesian hierarchical Gaussian processes (HGP) have shown great potential in OOS detection, particularly when dealing with complex, non-Gaussian data sets, by leveraging the simulations to derive probabilistic distributions for unknown variables in the model. Nonetheless, the implementation of B HGP involves a high degree of computational complexity, particularly during the estimation of probabilistic distributions for unknown variables in the model. 

In order to address these challenges and enhance computational efficiency, this study introduces a simplified framework for OOS detection, known as the Distributional Gaussian Processes (DGP) model. Unlike its predecessor, the B HGP model, the DGP model achieves increased efficiency by directly approximating the probabilistic distributions for unknown variables, while maintaining an accurate representation of data anomalies. 
Furthermore, this study demonstrates the efficacy of the DGP model in OOS detection by conducting rigorous simulations across multiple scenarios. By comparing the performance of the DGP model with existing techniques, including KS, B HGP, and Distributional Latent Function Models (DLFM), this research finds that the DGP model boasts superior computational efficiency and accuracy in detecting OOS

The effect of heat generated through periodic changes in a quantum system subject to external driving and boundary conditions is an unresolved issue. Researchers have demonstrated that this type of heating can be utilized to create ordered structures in isolated quantum systems. However, the same approach fails to produce such results in open quantum systems due to their tendency to lose and gain energy with their surroundings, leading to a lack of permanent order. In this research, we show that by trapping energy in a special state of a quantum system subject to external driving and boundary conditions, we can achieve robust aggregation in an otherwise unstable part of the system's energy spectrum, ultimately resulting in aggregate particle behavior. We studied this phenomenon in a one-dimensional system of bosons subject to external driving and boundary conditions, observing similar patterns in systems of varying sizes. By analyzing the system's behavior, we found that this phenomenon occurs due to the formation of a temporary, self-sustaining state, also known as a Floquet-scars, which traps energy in an otherwise unstable part of the system's energy spectrum, leading to aggregate particle behavior.

We derive novel and comprehensive estimates for the second symmetric derivative of solutions to the Monge--Amp\`ere equation, under a specified boundary constraint, in the context of convex polygons. These estimates demonstrate uniform second symmetric derivative estimates for convex solutions to this equation, assuming the boundary constraint is either an ellipsoid or a log-convex function, in the space of continuously differentiable functions.

Repeating optical pulse trains, necessary for optical clocks, are rare in nature, yet one finding of experimental studies is the presence of irregular fluctuations in phase. These irregular fluctuations arise from distinct mechanical systems and, from a mathematical perspective, can be broken down into two components: variations in phase, and the overall time spacing between pulses. Due to the logical connection between time and frequency, analyzing the time spacing of optical pulses provides valuable information about the irregular fluctuations in optical clocks. From a mathematical standpoint, we analyze random pulse delay distributions using stationary random functions, and show that one such function can completely describe the time domain behavior of optical black clocks. Additionally, we clarify the connection between continuous and discrete time models, and prove that a Markov random function is the most flexible representation of time domain behavior. However, this representation has a drawback of being nonunique, and we devise a method to overcome this flaw. Furthermore, we utilize the properties of stationary random functions to establish the stability of our time domain model, and show its applicability in frequency-swept lasers.

Software-defined networking (SDN) offers an innovative solution with the ability to break traditional network barriers. The industry has been working on developing standardized service-level agreements for network resources, but realizing real-time service delivery remains a challenge due to issues like fault detection, inventory management, contract monitoring, and resource allocation. The industry has proposed Fog computing as an alternative, allowing applications to seamlessly manage resources, but the concept remains in its infancy. In an effort to overcome these obstacles, this research proposes a multi-faceted approach, incorporating collaborative failure recovery, fault avoidance, and efficient resource management to enable real-time service delivery, on-time reconfigurations, and optimal resource utilization, all within the bounds of industry standards. The approach allows services to be managed in real-time, as evidenced by our experimental framework and the results showing improved network efficiency and reduced overheads. The industry-standard compliant architecture has also been validated and produced promising outcomes in our experimentation.

Deep neural networks' training involves adjusting their weight parameters through gradient-based optimization using a loss function that incorporates gradient manipulation. The performance of networks is significantly impacted by the loss function employed. This study examines the outcomes of various loss functions for neural networks by modifying the gradient manipulation process. The investigation focuses on two scenarios: one where the gradient is passed backwards undisturbed and another where the gradient is manipulated before being passed backwards. The findings indicate that different loss functions yield distinct outcomes for the gradient manipulation scenario, unlike the unchanged gradient scenario. It is also observed that certain loss functions are more suitable for the unchanged gradient scenario than others. Notably, the loss function is more dependent on the gradient manipulation method than on the used dataset. The method of gradient manipulation was found to outperform other methods in changing the loss function's impact. Additionally, the method of gradient manipulation was found to be more versatile than other methods as it can simulate other methods' effects on the loss function. As a result, the method of gradient manipulation can produce changes in the loss function's behavior for different models, which in turn affects the model's performance.

In the context of holographic error correction schemes, which can be used in holographic dualities such as EA duality, to address the black hole information problem and the ability to divide systems into their local and non-local components, we explore a new class of codes called hyper-invariant pyramidal quantum codes. These codes are created by applying the hyper-RASTA principle, a modification of the raSTA principle previously introduced, to a specific type of quantum circuit called RASTA codes. By using a unique combination of principles, such as condensed matter properties, geometric expansions, and 1-wire mappings, we can generate a systematic method to divide systems into their local and non-local components, thus enabling the division of systems into their ebit, qubit, or qudit forms. These codes are special types of quantum codes that have distinct properties, such as the ability to be divided into their local and non-local components, and the ability to be used as a physical layer in quantum computers. A new approach to creating quantum Prisoner's Dilemma games, such as the GHZ triangle code, is also presented, demonstrating how these codes can be used to create complex quantum entities from simpler components.

Previous studies of the Nuclei of Galaxies (NOG) revealed that a central fiber in a nucleus exhibits greater brightness than surrounding fibers, and that there are distinct populations of bright and dim fibers.  Research published in 2013 focused on the number of central fibers present in each galaxy, and found a statistical correlation in which the probability of a galaxy having n bright fibers is equal to the probability of a galaxy having m dim fibers, and n+m equals 5, with both n and m ranging from 0 to 5.  In order to further investigate these findings, this study quantifies the distance between bright fibers in a certain subgroup of galaxies with 5 bright fibers, by examining two characteristics: the probability that two bright fibers occupy adjacent galaxies, and the average distance between bright fibers, determined by averaging the distances between all possible pairs of bright fibers in these galaxies.  The results from 229 galaxies with 5 bright fibers, along with 229 corresponding dim fibers, indicate a 32% chance that two bright fibers occupy adjacent galaxies, and reveal an average distance between bright fibers of approximately 3.  By applying a Gaussian convolution for each value of n, the research thenons, and reveals an overall standard deviation of approximately 1.  The conclusions from this study further validate the theory that a galaxy's central fiber population is randomly divided into two distinct, uniformly distributed groups, each of which exhibits unique and distinguishable characteristics.

The rising interest in distributed energy resources has led to an increase in electricity consumption through smarter networks, resulting in a more complex management requirement for their distribution. Many advanced distribution management systems have been developed to take full advantage of the active network infrastructure by utilizing the characteristics of various distributed energy resources and load responses. Specifically, we are focusing on the application of the ideal conservation voltage reduction technique for active networks, which aims to maximize the generation from distributed energy resources within the network while minimizing the required reduction in consumption.

Although several methods have been proposed for implementing conservation voltage reduction on distributed networks, they are often centralized and fail to consider the inherent non-linear interactions between energy resources and load responses within distributed systems. Moreover, the growing number of distributed energy resources and smart devices has created significant communication and control constraints that need to be addressed. To resolve these issues, we are proposing a distributed ideal conservation voltage dimmer (DICVDim) to manage distributed energy resources and load responses proactively, taking into account non-linear interactions and constraints on communication and control processes.

By analyzing the dynamics of power flow, we are formulating a non-linear two-time-scale stochastic optimal strategy for managing the active distribution network in full capacity, which includes a variety of distributed energy resources and load responses. We are also developing a distributed algorithm with a dual structure for stochastic conservation voltage dimming, which allows energy resource companies to set fair standards for active network distribution and enable collaborative management of distributed energy resources and load responses by the network operator. Notably

We investigate a multi-armed bandit issue in the setting of expert advice. The experts' advice for each round is generated at random from a specific distribution that's the same for all times and arms. The draw of each expert's advice is an independent event. Notably, this random-draw setting is significantly distinct from a well-studied, nonrandom-draw setting found in prior research. In response, we develop an algorithm, called the Waiting-to-Learn algorithm, incorporating an 'expectation-maximization' technique. The algorithm is shown to have an optimal upper bound of the expected regret, which improves upon existing regret bounds for nonrandom draws. Furthermore, we find that our algorithm is effective even in a unique drawing scenario where certain conditions are met, resulting in a zero-expected regret in such instances. Lastly, we extend our algorithm to function well in scenarios where multiple experts provide delayed advice for each round.

I present an argument for utilizing generative models in the production of text, specifically in the area of natural language processing, where advancements in the field of computer vision have not yet translated to comparable gains. The primary obstacles to overcome include the inherent intricacies of natural language, which is compounded by the precision and subtlety of human expression. The following sections provide a critique of the status quo, an explanation of a proposed system called LEATHER, a framework for acquiring knowledge through the analysis of a broad and eclectical range of texts, which is designed to produce written content that mirrors human writing. LEATHER is comprised of the following elements: (a) a method for breaking down written content into basic components, which are used to categorize texts (c) a technique for generating new written content based on categorized examples (b) a rule-based approach to combining individual elements. The LEATHER system is outlined in Section 7, with discussions of related prior research in the field (1) studies highlighting the distinct elements of written content found in conversational dialogue (2) a survey of techniques for producing written content by machines. An in-depth examination of the LEATHER system is provided in Section 8, which includes a detailed example. The potential of the LEATHER system to produce new written content is described in Section 9, along with several potential applications. The paper concludes with a discussion of the LEATHER system in Section 10.

Following World War II, researchers in the field of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) built upon the work of Murray Gell-Mann and the theory of partons. They explored how the theory behaves under conditions of high temperature and density, in the context of heavy-ion collisions. Our understanding of this has been shaped by the work of Wilson, who in the 1960s developed lattice QCD as a way to regulate the theoretical calculations. Since then, numerous researchers have contributed to the field, leveraging increasing computational power to refine their results, ultimately confirming the predictions of the phase transition temperature and quark mass.

In this article, we review the progress made so far in the field of lattice QCD from the 1970s to the 1990s, specifically exploring thermal and dense matter. We focus on the development of this field and its underlying methods and techniques, rather than its applications. We begin with an overview of continuum QCD, before discussing lattice QCD and its underlying principles. We then review Gaugino calculations, before delving into the results of QCD with temperature and chemical potential. We conclude this section by addressing the challenges associated with lattice QCD and its solutions, before reviewing the results of lattice QCD and Quantum Chromodynamics. Finally, we conclude this article with a series of outlooks on various research topics in the field of lattice QCD and its predictions, ultimately concluding that the study of the QCD phase transition has been well-established and is now well

We innovate in the probabilistic modeling of mechanical stiffness by introducing a dynamic approach, capturing both transient and operational variations.
Through complex simulations, a neural-kernel that accurately represents time-dependent stress is derived, yielding precise results.
By utilizing offshore wind-turbine stress data from ADBM, an array of linked Gaussian Process models is established, providing a universal proxy that links loads to design stresses, thereby allowing prediction of mechanical stiffness.
This robust, scalable, and efficient framework can be widely applied, especially in the assessment of designing stiffs for large systems.

Following a major earthquake in Izmir, Turkey on October 30$^{rd}$, 2021,
social media platforms became a vital outlet for updating information regarding
the aftermath of the disaster and relief efforts. The sheer volume of data
posted on these platforms makes it an ideal source of insights, yet analyzing
it proves to be a substantial challenge due to the variety of user-generated
content. Consequently, the goal of this study is to develop a weighted
framework, grounded in Twitter data analysis theory, to categorize and
assign keywords related to the Izmir earthquake and aid search operations.
By utilizing the K-means clustering algorithm without pre-determining the number
of clusters, our method successfully extracted valuable information from raw
data. The accuracy of the clustering process was confirmed by examining the
tweets and identifying the dominant keywords in each group.

The $R_\infty$-character of a group, a function mapping group elements to real numbers, can be used to study finite quotients of uncountable groups like the Baumslag-Solitar group, a type of solvable group. By investigating how these quotients change when passing to lower levels of finite quotients, we establish parameters, known as $R_\infty$-invariants, to characterize all solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups, determining their nilpotency and finding them classified in a hierarchical framework. This study also leads to a characterization of solvable finite Baumslag-Solitar groups in terms of a specific property.

A new technique is developed to extract high-resolution structures from time-resolved experiments with uncertain data, leveraging an advanced optimization strategy that relies on a realistic atomistic model. This approach, known as forward-optimization, simulates the experiment by adjusting a few key factors and uses it in conjunction with an optimization algorithm to find the most accurate interpretation of experimental results. It is successfully tested on solving a 2D experiment with uncertain data and used to investigate the dynamics of a chemical reaction involving a ring-like molecule. This approach provides more accurate and reliable structures compared to other methods and is extendable to other experiments and systems.

Automated driving systems rely heavily on naturalistic driving datasets to develop and improve their capabilities, but there is a notable shortage of freely accessible data in this field. To bridge this gap, this research presents SceNDD, a new naturalistic driving dataset, gathered on expressways and urban routes, accompanied by multi-modal contextual information. In contrast to other datasets, SceNDD includes a broader range of sensors and data from diverse driving scenarios, as captured by a double dashboard-mounted camera system. To facilitate easier data analysis, a custom post-processing tool was employed to optimize the camera feeds, reducing the background noise from vehicle assets. This dataset was used to train a supervised model for object detection, as demonstrated by the accompanying evaluation results.

In this research, we introduce a new concept in our work on boundary/conformal field models, specifically reflected entropy, that is analogous to rationality in the context of one-dimensional systems and exhibits a similar consistency requirement. Building on this concept, we investigate the underlying reason for the consistency and derive a precise formula for reflected entropy that is relevant to both one-dimensional systems and two-dimensional models with interfaces. Furthermore, we provide supporting examples and evidence for the case of minimal models.

In order to enhance the performance of REML-based channel estimation in RIS-supported OFDM systems with limited CP and hardware inaccuracies, a deep learning-based alternative is presented. The enhanced algorithm incorporates an affine transformation to rectify distorted low-dimension channel data, thereby boosting its precision. The performance of the suggested method is demonstrated through simulations, indicating a significant enhancement over the original REML approach. Specifically, the results indicate that our solution achieves up to 3.5 more accurate low-dimension channel data and 75% more accurate users' SP propagation than the original REML method. Furthermore, the simulations reveal that our solution outperforms REML in terms of 90% of the cases and also in terms of output data accuracy when there are 4 or more extra zero elements in the RIS. The simulations also show that our solution outperforms REML in terms of performance even with perfect low-dimension channel data but with hardware inaccuracies present.

We propose a theoretical model to evaluate the contribution of distinct components within a system to its total energy by using the non-equilibrium statistical measure of work. Our findings reveal that the work performed by an external force agent can be calculated as the sum of its individual contributions from multiple dynamic components, under the condition that these components are non-interacting. Conversely, in cases of interacting components, the contribution of each element to the total work performed by the external agent cannot be calculated solely based on their separate dynamic behaviors, highlighting the complexity involved. Additionally, an extension of the second law for systems comprising multiple components shows that the total entropy generated is less than the sum of the entropies produced by individual elements, under the condition of non-interacting components.

We're exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A key breakthrough reveals that the deformation space of an instanton is an infinitesimal extension of the deformation space of an almost Hermitian structure. This result holds significant value, particularly in the case of a Kalb-Rubin surface, where the deformation space of the instanton is substantially larger than that of the underlying almost complex structure.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, many countries implemented strict measures such as stay-at-home orders, hand sanitizer requirements, and mask mandates to slow the virus's spread. In an effort to contain the outbreak, national health authorities created contact tracing systems to monitor individuals who may have come into close contact with someone infected with the virus. These Contact Trace Systems (CTSs) have gained significant attention, with various countries developing their own models, such as Singapore's MOH CV, the UK's Contact Trace England, the US's COVID-19 Contact Tracking, and Brazil's Coronav SUS CTC. The Coronav SUS CTS (hereinafter, RCS), employed by Brazil's federal government, stands out from its international counterparts by utilizing an untested technology. This study critically evaluates the confidentiality of the RCS to protect users' sensitive data, identifying not only a confirmed confidentiality breach but also a related security vulnerability that could enable near-undetectable Denial-of-Service attacks. Furthermore, when the RCS's data storage is viewed as a whole, this study identifies an information leakage risk to users' privacy. To address these concerns, this work offers concrete recommendations for enhancing the RCS's security and privacy. In an effort to promote the development of similar good security and privacy practices in other CTSs, this study also presents a set of universally applicable principles and recommendations for CTSs specifically designed to combat public health crises like the COVID-19 pandemic.

The application of quantum mechanics in neural networks for processing data is an emerging area of research. This book explores the use of quantum principles in data analysis by first addressing the fundamental question of how quantum states can be applied to discrete data. It demonstrates that quantum mechanics is a natural framework for information, particularly when dealing with correlations and superpositions, but faces limitations in continuous data. The following chapters focus on quantum circuits for data representation, techniques for data encoding, and the application of quantum mechanics in machine learning, covering topics such as basic operations, matrix representation, and the quantum computing equivalent of neural networks. The book also delves into the use of quantum mechanics in loss functions and regularization and concludes by examining the prospects for further advancements in this field.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically creating C code from ACL2 specifications. The process involves a C model embedded within ACL2, which enables the tool to produce a refined version of the C model consistent with the user's specifications. A reasoner is employed to ensure the correctness of the C model's refinement. We demonstrate the tool's effectiveness through a handful of examples and discuss its potential limitations. Furthermore, we investigate the potential challenges in utilizing the tool for large-scale programming and explore ways to address these challenges.

A cluster analysis was conducted on 39 members of the 39991 asteroid family, spanning a 20-minute time period, to study their orbital dynamics in detail. Their motion can be broken down into two distinct components - a uniform, steady state and a fluctuating pattern characterized by periodic oscillations. A thorough examination of the fluctuations revealed a strong correlation with the motion of the Ceres, suggesting a possible link to the Gravitational influence of the 2:1 Kirkwood gap. A mathematical model was developed to express these fluctuations in terms of the motion at the perihelion of the planets in the region. Notably, the presence of multiple resonance relationships with multiple asteroids, including a 1:N gravo-synchronous configuration with Haumea, was discovered. A thorough analysis of the (4852) Karila/90406/1991 TE2 gravo-synchronous family provided a mathematical framework to study these resonance relationships, offering valuable insights into the dynamics of the system. A comparison with existing asteroid families in the region revealed a unique pattern of motion in the Iochroma family members, suggesting that their motion is influenced by the gravitational pull of a larger, unidentified body in the system.

Building on Ramanujan's work with the discriminant of cubic forms, this research applies a similar approach to investigate the discriminant of the quadratic form associated with the Hurwitz zeta function, specifically for values of zeta($s$) where zeta($s$) lies in a particular complex family and s is real. This investigation will utilize both analytical and numerical methods to establish relationships between entries of a specific matrix, which is derived from the discriminant of the quadratic form, and will further use these results to provide insights into the behavior of the discriminant of the quadratic form in different parameter scenarios. Along the way, the method will be expanded to allow for a generalization of Ramanujan's original result and a more comprehensive understanding of the behavior of the discriminant of the quadratic form, and ultimately, the behavior of the Hurwitz zeta function itself.

We investigate a complex elliptic cohomology theory, based on equivariant algebras from the theory of bootstraps, that we believe addresses a long-standing conjecture of Freed and Hopkins about a particular kind of cohomology theory. This theory is related to a complex of differential graded algebras that is defined by polynomials from the Weyl algebra, is equivariant with respect to rotations and circle actions, and is based on the complex projective space's vector space V, thus forming CP(V). This new theory is called LEC, and we show it is isomorphic to a particular case of the theoretical framework on the based loop space of S2 considered by Bahelt. LEC can also be generalized to the vector space covariant version, LECC, by applying a process called coupling, and we establish that LECC is connected to a particular kind of cohomology,  Novikov elliptic cohomology, thus establishing a relationship with Konig's conjecture about the relationship between these two cohomology theories and the theoretical framework on the based loop space of S2.

We employ machine learning techniques to build a topological map of the Universe's connective structure, based on the principles of algebraic topology. This approach connects deep mathematical concepts, such as sheaves and simplicial complexes, to practical applications in physics through machine learning. A sheaf machine learns to capture the contiguity relations of geometric objects, thereby reconstructing the underlying topological structure of the matter field. By incorporating this topology into a physical theory, the resulting mathematical framework shares a resemblance with established theories in physics, like gauge theory coupled to a topological field. A sheaf-based framework can then be used to investigate properties of non-linear quantum systems, such as their mesoscopic behavior, even when individual constituents are inaccessible to physical observation. Recent research applied this method to the study of liquid crystals and the description of mesoscopic phases in quasi two-dimensional systems, yielding results that align with experimental findings in the field of soft condensed matter physics. This study marks a pivotal moment in the use of algebraic topology as a tool for data analysis in physics, offering a unique approach that integrates multiple scales and disciplines within the field.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of the angular distributions in the $J/\psi + c$ states produced through $e^+e^-\to J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) processes. The study is based on the Belle data, which features 93.00 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity collected at the $\Upsilon$(4S) resonance. This analysis ultimately leads to a refined determination of the $J/\psi$ polarization, yielding a more accurate value of $\hat{f}_{0} = 0.25 \pm 0.17_{\rm stat} ± 0.03_{\rm syst} ± 0.03(photon\ radiative\ corrections)$ when considering the non-relativistic QCD model and $-0.82 \pm 0.17_{\rm stat} ± 0.03_{\rm syst} ± 0.03(photon\ radiative\ corrections)$ when adopting the color-singlet model.

Our past research revealed that Signal PINs were vulnerable to brute-force attacks, which led the developers to remove the feature from the application. Contrary to the assumption that this move was influenced by user preferences, our current investigation found no evidence that users preferred to abandon the PINs. A online survey of 228 Signal users aged 18-75 with varying levels of education, conducted in English and Spanish, showed that users were not in favor of the PINs either. The majority of the participants, both casual and enthusiastic users, were unaware of the reason behind the PINs' removal and had difficulties understanding how security measures could be compromised by user actions. This study suggests a lack of security education as a possible reason for the PINs' removal and presents possible future research on how to educate users with basic and advanced internet skills about security for everyone.

The integration of point-wise functions over the solar irradiance spectrum, weighted by Gaussian distributions, yields accurate results for solar energy calculations. A new table of solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature values has been developed, offering improved precision compared to existing ones. By using this table, users can efficiently obtain highly accurate integrals with minimal computational effort. A companion Julia software package'solarweights' provides access to this data and supports calculations in multiple programming languages, including Julia, MATLAB, Python, R, and Julia/NumPy.

The curvature based learning methods recent advancements hold crucial advantages in fast convergence and adaptive learning processes. This study thoroughly examines the complex structure of the curvature derived from the Hessian or Generalized Hessian. It is discovered that these curvatures inherently contain a variable dimensional component known as the Fisher Information, which governs the curvature's singular behavior and identifies its curvature null-space. Through the connection made with the Natural Gradient method, a low dimensional structure is established within the curvature derived from the Generalized Gauss-Newton. This leads to the development of the ViViT objective, offering a training procedure that is both efficient and scalable to scenarios involving complex architectures and high dimensionality, while also facilitating the incorporation of constraints. Experimental evaluations with various models and datasets demonstrate the exceptional performance of the ViViT objective in optimizing learning processes.

Many languages categorize nouns by grammatical gender, which enables a unique opportunity to examine how this categorization impacts how we represent nouns in space. We investigated this phenomenon by analyzing how the grammatical gender of nouns impacts their word embeddings in languages that utilize gender as a key categorization feature. Our research primarily links Grammatical Gender to Neutral Gender in these languages, comparing them to languages that classify nouns by Natural Gender. We discovered that the grammatical gender of nouns is associated with a significant, systematic shift in their direction within the word embedding space. We established a comprehensive framework to explain this phenomenon, incorporating aspects of conceptual metaphors, cultural factors, and the structure of human cognition.

We demonstrate that the special linear group SLn(R) exhibits charm within its charactristic subgroup framework, building on work by Buczynski and Platsopoulos. Our 'charability' finding hinges on a particular division of SLn(R) into subgroups, achieved through a generalization of Klaff and Rudnick's projective action equidistribution theorem to the realm of characteristic subgroups.

Zero-Shot class-level image analysis involves estimating an image's semantic composition without relying on any pre-training or prior knowledge. In contrast, we are exploring Zero-Shot class-level object position estimation, which requires pinpointing the class-level object's precise location without any prior training. To achieve this, we propose a novel framework consisting of two stages: firstly, detecting individual classes and localizing grounds truth; secondly, determining the ground truth class and estimating its position based on an embedding-driven approach. Our framework, orphaned from conventional supervision during training, astonishingly achieves impressive results on the ADE20K dataset, boasting an accuracy rate of 36.2%!

Traffic engineers rely on traffic forecasting to optimize transportation systems, but current methods often struggle to accommodate large datasets or real-time data due to limitations of early models. The typical solution involves applying machine learning models to predict traffic conditions, yet these models typically require substantial training data. To address this issue, this paper proposes the Application-driven Traffic Forecasting framework (AFORCAST), a novel approach based on sparsity and semantic similarity that enables reliable traffic prediction in extensive areas with limited data availability. The framework consists of two parts: the sparse traffic representation learning module and the similarity-driven prediction module. By utilizing the latent sparsity representation, the similarity-driven prediction module can compile local and global data, leading to more accurate predictions. We evaluated AFORCAST on a real-world dataset and found it outperformed popular machine learning models and existing traffic forecasting approaches.

Recent advances in causal deep learning have primarily focused on addressing one key issue: determining causal relationships between variables. In contrast, this study centers around generating causal relationships, aiming to identify the underlying mechanisms that allow us to manipulate one variable and observe changes in another. To accomplish this, we developed variational graph autoencoders (VACEs) to optimize two objectives: a variational counterfactual likelihood and cross-entropy for predicting the intervention target. Our experiments show that VACEs surpass existing methods in learning causal relationships and can effectively produce interventions and generate counterfactual scenarios. Moreover, our analysis reveals that variational counterfactual likelihood encourages the network to incorporate uncertainty while working with latent variables.

Our REALTA system captures Far Far Far Near Far Far Far Near Far Near Far Near Far Near Far Near Far Near Far Near Far Near Far Near Far Near Far Near Far Near Far data in real-time from the Irish LOFAR station (I-LOFAR) every 30 seconds. This enables a fast response time for follow-up observations with other facilities. The system underwent a full test during a notable gamma-ray burst, GRB210228A. The alert was issued at 19:424.35 UTC, 30 seconds after the detection by the Gamma-ray Burst Coordinate Network (GBN), utilizing a single neutrino converter in the I-LOFAR array. The issue was then confirmed by the European VLBI Network (EVN) at 20:00:15 UTC, demonstrating the effectiveness of REALTA in coordinating multi-instrument follow-up observations.

We suggest articulating the mission of metamaterials research as it pertains to photon dynamics, referring to the area as 'clever metaphotonics'. This term encapsulates the core challenge of accurately predicting and understanding how light behaves when interacting with man-made structures that manipulate light waves. By redefining the problem in this way, the application of machine learning techniques becomes more accessible for addressing traditional metamaterials queries. Furthermore, the use of machine learning is essential for exploring the vast possible landscape of artificial structures that can be designed. Specifically, the integration of neural networks plays a critical role in the successful execution of the mission of metaphotonics. This incorporation of neural networks enables the simulation of artificial structures that may not have been previously considered, thereby guiding research towards more targeted goals. By cross-referencing theoretical simulations with experimental measurements, the accuracy of metaphotonics predictions can be validated. Ultimately, the incorporation of neural networks is instrumental in propelling the metaphotonics field forward, offering tangible outcomes such as the identification of optimal artificial structures that can be used in applications like sensing, lighting, and solar energy.

The primary goal of this research is to evaluate how much the initial release of key cinematic attributes, such as visual effects, music, and 3D technology, influenced the financial success of films in the analysis. Our method combines an expanded dataset of 743 films with a more sophisticated statistical analysis. By utilizing a novel likelihood-based test, we identified that visual effects significantly impacted revenue, with financial investments in visual effects leading to higher box office returns. Our findings also revealed that breaking 3D into a categorical variable enhances the accuracy of our predictive model. Although the financial value of music and seamless integration to 3D were not supported by our data, we justified the continued importance of these factors in the analysis. Our research indicates that including these attributes early on can boost a film's box office returns, though the financial benefits of such decisions may be subjective.

The integration of widespread distributed energy resources has fundamentally altered the dynamic behavior of power grids.  To manage this transformation, a crucial issue arises when the conventional frequency stabilization mechanism is removed, leading to potential instability in the power system.  This instability issue is also observed in high penetration renewable energy scenarios.  This research paper evaluates the effect of frequency stabilization on the voltage stability and presents a new method, an auxiliary frequency stabilization approach, to enhance voltage stability by utilizing the existing power system equipment as voltage control devices.  The proposed technical solution has been implemented on a test 11 kV distribution grid in Gangnam, Seoul, and has shown effective performance by maintaining both system voltage and frequency within specified limits.

Cyberphysical networks are crucial for interconnecting and coordinating large numbers of distributed control and automation systems within an organization's operational framework, aligning with the envisioned global cyberphysical machine. The development of autonomous cyberphysical agents is key to handling the ever-increasing complexity involved in system design, operation, and maintenance. Building such agents requires the integration of diverse, often disparate technology elements, which necessitates a unified approach, exemplified in this paper. A cognitive architecture is proposed, incorporating multiple cognitive agents to facilitate systemic reflection, depending on the system's design. The approach is demonstrated through a universal cognitive diagram and a case study involving a network of industrial systems.

Inverse Compton radiation in blarars, particularly in the UV and X-ray ranges, is a complex process influenced by the variable and non-stable optical and near-infrared radiation emanating from their jets. Since this radiation is polarized, it has a detectable impact on the IC spectrum, which can be measured. Our study, building on a previous one, has created a code to simulate IC scattering of non-polarized and polarized radiation, which was then used to analyze the spectral data of 12 blarars obtained through the XMM-Newton telescope. The results indicate that our MAPPIES code accurately identifies specific optical and near-infrared radiation energies based on XMM-Newton data and multiple observational data types. Our study of these 12 blarars revealed various patterns, with a specific correlation observed between a specific surplus in the XMM-Newton data and the shape of the XMM-Newton quiescent flux in the 0.3 to 1 keV range, which was observed in 9 out of 12 blarars. The majority of these 12 blarars were observed to have a specific polarization characteristic in the XMM-Newton data, which was discovered to be a potential marker for these jets. The results of our study suggest that these 12 blarars are experiencing a specific emission mechanism, which could involve a specific radiation interaction based on the non-polarized and polarized radiation observed. Research on complex terrains aims to extend the concept of complex manifolds to terrain models, which may have features like valleys, plateaus, and peaks. In this study, we explore the extension of analytic functions on such diverse landscapes. A valley in this context refers to a particular type of generalised valency region introduced by the researcher (see [Valuation rings over compact analytic manifolds and complex terrains, arXiv:2101.00722]). We establish that analytic functions can be freely expanded in the mentioned landscapes, which are a subset of complex terrains. This finding aligns with existing results for smooth surfaces and three-dimensional spaces. Additionally, we demonstrate that our subset of landscapes includes all polyhedrons defined by the decomposition of Minkowski space into convex regions.

We'll investigate the virtual detection of pure states with symmetric components.
Virtual detection involves measuring a quantum system without actually being in that state.
This process can be conceptualized as post-selectively measuring an entangled system formed from the state and an additional reference state.
Our research delves into three different scenarios where we analyze various properties of the measured system's spectrum.
These investigations lead us to understand how local filtering of a multi-partent state can be seen as a specific type of entanglement-based measurement.
Furthermore, our analysis reveals that certain states cannot be virtually detected and leads us to a broader understanding of the definition of a nullity.

We're investigating the process of baryon creation through the quantization of a QCD string that undergoes an oscillatory failure. This string, characterized by oscillatory failures with a wavelength of 17, 25, 31 units (in string units), is exemplified by a three-helix string with mass $m_u=m_d=m_d^*$, where $m_d^*$ differs from $m_d$. By employing a finite interval of a $Poincar\'e$ map, that encompasses three zero-points, we can explain the partonization process that leads to the creation of baryons in terms of open QCD strings that exhibit distinct modes of vibration. In contrast to the previously considered $Poincar\'e$ map that encompasses one only zero-point, the present description yields three types of excitations each corresponding to one of the three helices. This consideration is tied to the breakdown of the GUT symmetry by the edge interaction that causes distinct splittings of the QCD string into three separate parts.

The way energy is moved within and circulated around the sun's tachocline layer has a significant influence on the type of waves detected in the sun's atmosphere through helioseismic imaging. Any differences between the observed behavior of these waves and predicted models may indicate the presence of dynamic processes such as mass changes or rotation variations within the sun's interior. Specifically, studies have found discrepancies in the sun's rotation at its surface and inner layers, and to investigate the role of circulating currents in these discrepancies, researchers used a three-dimensional sun model that simulated various currents and mass effects to see how they impact wave travel times. They found that when circulating currents were part of the model, it significantly altered the observed travel times, contrary to predictions made by one-dimensional models. Furthermore, the researchers discovered that circulating currents could explain a significant portion of the observed delay in travel times found through helioseismic imaging.

High-redshift sources emit their gravitational waves at lower frequencies due to the universe's expansion. Researchers believe that primordial magnetic fields in large-scale structures could be one such source, leading to a signal that can be detected with future instruments like the NANOGrav dataset. The prediction of this signal relies on assumptions regarding its power-law characteristics and the magnetic field's evolution, yielding significantly more stringent constraints on the early universe's magnetic properties than previously possible.

Light field images contain the cross-view spatial information, generating a substantial amount of data that poses a significant compression challenge. The standard image compression techniques fail to achieve desirable results when applied to light field images. To overcome this issue, a disintegration model that splits the cross-view spatial information into scene-related and spatially-dependent disparities was previously developed. This disintegration model enables the application of conventional image compression methods to the two distinct components, yielding superior results. Building upon this concept, a disparity-aware model for light field image compression is presented in this study. The model incorporates a learning-based component that simplifies the transformation of low-level pixel information into disparity maps. As a result, image representation efficiency is enhanced, and higher-quality compressed and decompressed light field images are yielded. The model performed competitively in objective metrics and user studies evaluating the perceived quality of compressed and decompressed light field images.

A key challenge in Cross-Language Information Retrieval (CLIR) arises from the difficulty of determining the optimal level of semantic representation of query and documents for comparison. Interactive CLIR overcomes this by asking users to specify document and query languages, but this comes with the limitation of being time-consuming and less suitable for large collections. On the other hand, a non-interactive approach avoids these constraints, yet struggles with the representation issue. Despite the non-interactive framework's potential, it has not received much attention in recent studies. Our work seeks to highlight the benefits of a combination approach – blending interactive and non-interactive CLIR techniques. Experiments conducted on the Standard Information Retrieval Framework (SIRF) dataset, which showcases multilingual documents, revealed that merging these methods slightly boosted retrieval performance in all tested scenarios and were particularly effective when the number of relevant documents was limited. Moreover, our findings indicate that employing vector transformers can bring benefits to CLIR, regardless of the approach used.

This paper explores the best practices for estimating models and designing surveys in the context of small-area estimation in low-income countries. The research finds that a detailed understanding of the survey dataset is essential, and suggests a step-by-step approach to estimation. The analysis evaluates the performance of different small-area estimation methods using simulated datasets, based on real data. The results indicate that Bayesian spatial models are a viable option, and offer a simple approach to small-area estimation. The research also identifies key factors to consider when selecting an estimation method and provides guidance for future small-area estimation projects in low-income countries.

We've developed a quantum version of the Kelly criterion for optimal betting, using continuous variable protocols in quantum processing systems. Our approach generates a new equation to determine optimal bet sizes, which can be calculated without simulating the noisy quantum process. By using the quantum process's output states, we've established a way to evaluate the expected wager limit. Our methods are suitable for scenarios where the quantum dynamics are uncertain, as long as the initial state is known. Moreover, when the initial state is also uncertain, we've created a way to determine optimal bet sizes based on the average outcome. Our research demonstrates that this quantum technique can surpass the optimal outcomes from the original Kelly criterion.

Recently, two-dimensional semiconductor MoSi$_4$N$_4$ has shown potential as an energy-efficient material for optoelectronics. However, the alignment of the energy levels of the quasiparticle and the interaction with electrodes in this material remain unclear. This study performs comprehensive first-principles calculations to investigate the quasiparticle energy alignment and interlayer properties of MoSi$_4$N$_4$, as well as similar compounds MoWe$_4$As$_4$, WeSi$_4$As$_4$, and TiGe$_4$As$_4$. A unique approach is taken by combining the quasiparticle energy and electrostatic potential, calculated using a finite electric field, in this study. The findings show that MoSi$_4$N$_4$ has an inherent characteristic where the interlayer quasiparticle energy discrepancy is eliminated, resulting in equally distributed energy. This characteristic is further proven to be independent of different stacking configurations in this study. As a result, MoSi$_4$N$_4$ can function as a common exciton across various MoSi$_4$N$_4$ orientations and layers. A similar energy alignment is discovered in the other studied compounds MoWe$_4$As$_4$ and WeSi$_4$As$_4$, suggesting that MoSi$_4$N$_4$'s properties can serve as a benchmark for understanding and predicting the quasiparticle and exciton behavior in the similar materials

A novel search for the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ is presented, with an analysis of the full Run 1 dataset collected by the LHCb experiment. A significance of $6.3 \sigma$ is achieved for this unusual decay, and the branching ratio is calculated as $(4.44 \pm 1.06) \times 10^{-8}$, assuming the standard model prediction. The findings are presented for both a dilepton invariant mass range and individual mass bins.

The beginning of a protoplanetary system's development is influenced by the breakdown and reorganization of its initial disk in an undisputed manner.  A new investigation explores how the extensive stellar cluster environment in young open clusters brings about the destruction of a prestellar core, triggering a planetary system's formation.  By using a simplified model of a three-in-one planetary system, researchers have calculated the evolution of its molecular composition, from the core's rupture to its completion, and discovered that the core's fragmentation into multiple parts greatly impacts gas and dust separation, resulting in the formation of a dusty ring surrounding a massive planet, and a gas-rich zone in the center, similar to an exoplanetary system.  They also found that planetary formation is not a one-time event and that small, irregular objects within the system continue to break apart and reassemble, enabling diversity and asymmetry in planetary systems that are not seen in exoplanetary systems.  Furthermore, the core's rupture leads to the emergence of hot and cool dust components, and it's hypothesized that these dust components are the initial steps in the formation of asteroids and comets, and possibly even the irregular surfaces of planets with highly irregular terrain.

In astronomy with large telescopes, atmospheric scattering poses a major challenge by diverting light away from the telescope, resulting in uneven light distribution across the field of view. Although existing models attempt to account for this effect, their accuracy varies significantly. To improve our understanding of atmospheric scattering, we conducted a study of a particular form of scattering called differential chromatic aberration correction, and identified the factors influencing its effectiveness. By simulating this effect under various conditions, we were able to establish a correlation between image brightness and color, and verify these predictions against actual observations made with a specific telescope under diverse atmospheric situations. Notably, our observations show a notable disparity between the scattering effect observed with a large telescope versus a smaller one, underscoring the importance of characterizing a telescope's point-spread function under different color conditions.

This paper tackles the problem of modeling complex temporal sequences with multiple components. The existing research framework relies on the assumption of independent and identically distributed data points, which often leads to inaccurate predictions. To address this issue, we propose a novel method that accounts for interactions between nearby data points, as well as global correlations within the data sequence. The proposed approach utilizes a novel Gaussian Bayes model, which incorporates element-wise advantages of logistic neural network and Gaussian process, to accurately model input sequences. The model's complexity is effectively managed by implementing Bayesian variational inference, which also enables the estimation of a dynamic matrix that learns from the data and adapts to changing states. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this method in forecasting future system states based on temporal sequences.

The Pontryagin duality principle has several thought-provoking implications that 
demonstrate the intricate balance between topological properties in various 
different spaces. This concept, originating from analysis, has found practical 
applications across multiple areas of mathematics. In this paper, I will highlight 
key examples of Pontryagin duality's influence on ongoing research in set theory, 
with a specific focus on continuous reasoning.

The distinction between administrative and criminal justice data involves both comprehensively detailed information and restricted access. Due to confidentiality concerns, the combined dataset remains unexplored, despite potential machine learning applications. Cross-domain federal learning offers a promising solution, as seen in early projects such as FedAbacus, aiming to study administrative data using a differential privacy framework. Our analysis shows that the combination of cross-domain and differential privacy, specifically the commonly used DP-FedSG approach, is vulnerable to external interference, as shown by adaptive attack examples. In contrast, the approach CP-FedSG, incorporating a communication protocol that includes channel encoding and decoding, offers enhanced protection against such attacks. Our research also includes comparative performance evaluations of both methods in terms of accuracy and learning efficiency. Ultimately, the article presents arguments in favor of utilizing differential confidentiality for sensitive data, including suggestions for future research direction.

We present a supersymmetric extension of the fundamental $U(1)_X$ model, characterized by one $Z_2$ and one $Z_2'$ R-charge, offering an explanation for dark matter and dark energy through right-handed neutrinos, without requiring an understanding of the dark sector. In this model, a minimal set of new fields and parameters is introduced, with the dark neutrino's mass solely dependent on the underlying $U(1)_X$ gauge coupling. Notably, a supersymmetric version of the Stueckelberg mechanism has been applied to generate a dark mass. Additionally, this model has been thoroughly analyzed for its theoretical and experimental validity, including the impact of new parameters on the dark sector. Furthermore, a complementary study has been conducted to investigate the influence of additional singlet fields on the dark matter properties, specifically when these fields are charged under $Z_2$ and $Z_2'$, a situation that often arises in supersymmetric models. Lastly, a representation of the underlying $U(1)_X$ gauge group has been adopted, featuring a minimal set of matter fields, thereby yielding a supersymmetric version of the fundamental $U(1)_X$ model introduced by Frampton.

We have developed a novel, highly efficient machine learning technique to boost the throughput of a wireless network assisted by intelligent surfaces, even when a device that interferes with energy transfer is present. To achieve this, we first use a conventional method to determine the optimal values of key parameters. Next, we design an efficient network model that models and computes the performance of different settings with minimal calculations. Finally, we create a system that generates useful data for training an effective function, utilizing an unsupervised learning technique to improve the function's output in a separate process. Our results show that our proposed approach greatly surpasses a comparative approach in terms of both computation speed and throughput.

For the first time since the discovery of neutron capture, researchers have observed the beta-plus-neutron decay of $186$Hg with a branch ratio of $3.1\pm0.3(10^{-4})$. They used this observation to determine the Boltzmann absolute ground state energy of the $186$Hg isotope as $771\pm$ 3 keV, which consisted of measurements from multiple experiments. Analyzing this energy, researchers were able to test various models that predict how particles interact at short ranges, and as a result, they found that the $186$Hg system slightly favors the formation of clusters in its nuclear structure.

Within the framework of the SU(5) grand unified theory, we examine the relationship between the 'dark substance' concept and the leptogenesis process in a unified manner. The 'dark substance' hypothesis suggests that the 125 GeV Higgs boson is comprised of a dark sector superfield, where a portion of the Higgs mass can be attributed to the dark sector's contribution to the radiative correction of the top quark pole mass. In this study, we leverage a unified framework that includes a right-handed neutrino and a dark sector superfield to explore the radiative correction of the top quark pole mass within the minimal supersymmetric SU(5) grand unified theory. The newly introduced parameters regulate both the dark substance and the magnitude of baryon number non-conservation during reheating, thereby influencing the generation of the baryon asymmetry of the universe. The model incorporates a right-handed neutrino-mediated neutrino mass generation mechanism and dark substance contribution to the Higgs potential at the Lagrangian level. Ultimately, we validate the model's viability by demonstrating its consistency with both the Planck satellite data and the 117-fold enhanced LHC dataset.

For applications involving autonomous robots, developing algorithms that produce robust results in realistic simulation environments is a primary concern, as successful outcomes may not translate to real-world settings. The focus has usually been on simulation performance rather than the actual real-world outcomes. The key challenge here is real-world implementation, which in robotic control terms, means achieving goal-directed state trajectories similar to those simulated. The complexity arises from the fact that achieving optimal real-world outcomes often requires more than just adjusting the simulation algorithm parameters. The main advantage of our approach is that it enables data-driven control with minimal reliance on prior knowledge and realistic simulation models. The feasibility of this approach is illustrated through various experiments, which show that our method enables dynamic tasks with unpredictable task properties and bypasses the limitation of requiring accurate world models, making it more practical for deployment. The study includes multiple scenarios such as a quadrotor performing different aerial maneuvers, a swimmer navigating through an unknown environment, and a robot completing an intricate task beyond conventional reach points. The results show promising performance in one-shot implementations on physical robots.

The Toda conformal quantum field theory based on $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ is analyzed with a focus on its integrable spin components. Our analysis involves the use of Affine Toda field theory with a specific mass parameter $m$ near the unitarity threshold. This is achieved through the application of a $1/m$ expansion. At the next order in the expansion, our calculations yield new ward relationships among the spin components of the Toda field. These results complement existing known relationships and support a unique duality at the next order in the expansion. Additionally, our analysis of the correlation functions across this 1/m expansion reveals a convergence pattern similar to that observed in the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ system. This implies that the leading terms in the 1/m expansion of the Toda correlation functions provide precise, universal descriptions of the non-perturbative properties of the system. Our analysis also extends the scope of the Toda conformal quantum field theory to include solutions involving the degenerate fields. These solutions apply equally to the systems near the threshold of unitarity and in the systems far from the threshold of unitarity. This is achieved through the application of a functional method. This is the first study to examine the properties of the spin components in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ system at the next order in the expansion. We introduce Connection Relation GAN, a novel approach that leverages structural connections among samples in an embedding space. Our approach, specifically designed for unsupervised learning, utilizes the structural connections between original data and its embedded representation. This method capitalizes on the benefits of regularizer in training neural networks by integrating a triplet loss minigun. The connection structure is inferred through a straightforward process with pre-existing neural networks, eliminating the need for complex architectural modifications. We conduct comprehensive experiments on two real-world datasets, ImageNet-1k and Food-10, to demonstrate that our approach produces visually acceptable and semantically meaningful results. These results highlight the potential of structural connections in improving GAN representations and lay the groundwork for future research in this direction.

A novel approach to quantum communication, twin-field key exchange (TFKE), offers a reliable method of secure data transfer between distant parties over long distances. Its key advantage lies in the ability to maintain a shared quantum state, but it requires precise synchronization of optical phase. Lacking this synchronization would result in reduced efficiency or complete failure of communication. To overcome this limitation, a new TFKE protocol has been developed, enabling stable data transfer in environments where conventional TFKE fails due to lack of phase synchronization.
