The proposed observed is theoretically proven to closely approximate the true system state under certain stringent conditions, and its effectiveness is further validated through numerous numerical experiments conducted using various fault models. The constructed observer also facilitates the realization of a proxy system that mimics the original non-linear system's behavior.

Recent research has employed transformer-based models on temporal knowledge graph completion (TKGC), a challenging domain. The motivation behind our work involves identifying if a more efficient approach using a fixed, state-of-the-art model can still excel on TKGC tasks. The connection prediction module of MotifTKGC, a well-performing TKGC method, shares similarities with the head and tail embedding generation in ConvE, another renowned TKGC method. Based on this insight, our research compares the prediction performance of MotifTKGC, ConvE, and a novel approach that integrates the fixed models into TKGC tasks. The results show that using a single, fixed model is a practical solution to achieve competitive results in TKGC.

Research on high-power ultrafast pulse generation using Kerr-lens mode-locking has typically focused on technique and then on the underlying physics, overlooking the essential role of geometric scaling in achieving this objective. In fact, achieving stable, high-energy pulse generation at low repetition rates often necessitates mode-locking cavity geometries that can accommodate multiple fundamental transverse modes, which in turn allows for the formation of spatial-temporal solitons across the cavity. These unique hybrid states have the capacity to adapt to variations in pump power and cavity temperature, thereby stabilizing the modelocking operation. In order to understand and potentially exploit geometric scaling for the development of new, high-energy pulse generation methods, our analysis commences with an in-depth examination of the geometric properties of one such hybrid entity, comprised of a transverse-pentagon laser cavity, containing three convex mirrors and four other curved components with varying degrees of curvature. In contrast, our own experimental and numerical investigations involve a linear cavity with six curved components having identical curvatures. As a result, our analysis reveals that geometric scaling can significantly enhance the laser pulse energy by an amount proportional to the square root of the ratio of the larger to the smaller curvature values, which explains the significantly greater performance achieved in our experiments using a linear cavity compared to a traditional non-geometric setup. In conclusion, our analysis has clearly demonstrated the essential contribution of geometric scaling to the development of high-energy pulse generation methods, and we anticipate that this finding can serve as a guiding

A growing trend in machine learning research, federated learning seeks to develop robust, data-hungry models using distributed client devices. Yet, a major challenge in FL arises from the varying computational capabilities and power limitations of these devices. To tackle this issue, our paper proposes a novel asynchronous framework for supporting both sustainable and efficient model training across diverse devices in parallel. The framework's key components include a cutting-edge nonlinear regression model, a distributed strategy for model selection and optimization, and adaptive mechanisms for balancing model convergence and computation time. Notably, our experiments show that this approach can achieve comparable performance to synchronous models, while also reducing training expenses and computation time by 29.2% and 18.4%, respectively. The findings, supported by comprehensive numerical tests, demonstrate the potential for efficient, distributed FL under resource constraints.

To optimize the absorption of solar irradiance by thin silicon layers with targeted thicknesses between 10 and 300nm, researchers investigated photonic band gap back reflectors in a setup assessing total absorption. Following a numerical model of the setup initially proposing unit total absorption for any silicon layer thickness, researchers modified the model to account for realistic photonic band gap reflectors with inherent absorption and edge roughness discontinuities. By re-evaluating the total absorption using a 2D model with rough boundaries, researchers found that thin layers benefit from 3D photonic band gap back reflectors more than ultra-thin layers. A comparison of calculation methods showed that both absorptive and reflective losses need to be taken into account to accurately determine the total absorption of thin silicon layers. Furthermore, the study found that thin layers benefit from 3D photonic band gap back reflectors more than ultra-thin layers, and that ultra-thin layers require either nano-pylons or hole structures to achieve maximum total absorption.

We take a holistic approach to solving one specific, yet complex, branch of the function y = c^^((x - c)) with the requirement that y = 1. This particular function is a crucial building block for solving higher-level algebraic equations, particularly those involving powers and exponents. Although the solution to this problem is straightforward at first glance, it has been the subject of much debate due to its inherent complexity. The existing literature offers a variety of methods to solve this equation, each with its unique strengths and limitations. The purpose of this study is to provide the most efficient solution possible, taking into account the specific limitations of each method. Furthermore, this paper will take a historical approach, critiquing the prior work of other mathematicians in this area and providing alternative perspectives. The primary contribution of this study is to identify and address the specific difficulties presented by this particular problem, ensuring that any proposed solutions are rigorous and accurate. The asymptotic behavior of the solution to the equation y = c^^((x - c)) is the central focus of this paper, and we divide the existing approaches into three distinct categories: those that can be applied directly, those that can be applied indirectly, and those that rely on auxiliary equations. By taking a unified approach to this problem, we believe that this study offers a more complete understanding of the function y = c^^((x - c)) and provides a comprehensive review of the theoretical tubular algebraic equations in general.

The M-estimation technique, used extensively in fields like finance and economics, suffers from slow convergence rates in high-dimensional environments.  In this study, a method called the cover expansion, which offers enhanced asymptotic convergence rates, is developed for non-differentiable convex M-estimation.  Cover expansion is effectively applied to a multi-stage convex program, yielding improved estimators.  Notably, this approach is free from issues present in existing methods such as the 'divide and conquer' technique, whose breakdown into smaller sub-problems leads to diminished performance in high-dimensional scenarios.  In this context, the cover expansion demonstrates the capability to combine smaller sub-problems in a high-dimensional setting, thus offering better convergence rates.  Comprehensive simulation experiments validate and confirm the theoretical analysis of the estimators derived from cover expansion.

Researchers investigated the magnetic properties of the cleavage-oriented, centered honeycomb antiferromagnet GdInO3 through comprehensive studies using magnetization, DC and AC susceptibility measurements, and detailed refinement of the crystallographic parameters.  This research found that the long-range magnetic order below 3.4 K is disrupted by significant disorder within the crystal structure, which is consistent at temperatures above 2 K.  Following a model that accounts for weak, non-uniform spin interactions, researchers were able to demonstrate that the observed magnetic behavior is accurately explained, even considering a weak, easy axis that aligns with the c-axis.  Furthermore, the temperature-dependent magnetic specific heat showed no distinct transitions, further indicating a two-dimensional magnetic phenotype.

Predicting missing connections in networks based on existing ones is a key use case for network analysis that the neural network method Simple Statistical Network Embedding (SSNE) has significantly improved. Nevertheless, SSNE's original formulation is not suitable for large, sparse networks as it is computationally intensive. To address this limitation, a new version of SSNE, referred to as Efficient Statistical Network Embedment (SSNEE), has been developed for such networks by optimizing the prediction process. To achieve this, SSNEE employs an alternative formulation that is inspired by the Swenson star expansion technique in the context of network analysis, thereby reducing the number of operations from O(n^2) to O(n) while also minimizing memory usage. Experimental findings on diverse networks of varying densities show that SSNEE outperforms the original SSNE method, not only in terms of computational efficiency, but also the quality of the embedding representations it produces, ultimately leading to enhanced edge prediction accuracy. A supporting demonstration is available at:  https://github.com/hoonS/SSNEE/embedder/Embedder.html.

Two-dimensional gas clouds with ultra-low dimensions and ultra-high densities,
referred to as atomic vapor sheets or gas sheets, have been successfully created
using a new technique incorporating micro-fabrication design and laser cooling.
This method employs a microchip-based vapor chamber to contain a mixture of
rubidium and cesium that has been cooled to a superfluid state of liquid
helium-4. By leveraging the microchip's integrated heat dissipation features,
temperature stabilization has been achieved at 50 seven digits of precision.
Observations include the presence of a gas sheet with one-millimeter width and
the detection of characteristic signature isotope shifts from interacting atoms,
along with measurements of their volume density, at around 10 to the power of
11 per cubic liter. This innovative approach enables the production of large
quantities of these specialized gas clouds, opening the door for integration with
microchips and integrated photonics, thus accelerating the development of
sophisticated quantum computers and precise clocks.

We develop mathematical models to calculate the nonlinear disruption distance of specially designed high-order spatial modes in dual-polarization formats, which are crucial for high-data-rate transmission in underwater optical communications. The studied formats are compatible with standard single-mode fiber transmission. The models incorporate the fundamental transverse mode's nonlinear threshold distance to convey the relationship between nonlinear disruption distance and channel bandwidth. The accuracy of the models is validated through simulations of dual-polarization 4D formats transmitted over 500 km, which achieve a combined spectral and spatial channel count of 32.

Large wildfires have been devastating global ecosystems, therefore predicting and tracking their progression has become increasingly crucial.  Satellite imagery is essential for monitoring these massive fires, providing valuable data on fire detection, visualization, and forecasting.  One major limitation of current satellite-based techniques is the need to switch between near-infrared and visible spectral images to track the extent of active flames.  To overcome this limitation and develop a more efficient imaging method, we propose a novel deep learning approach that combines multi-spectral infrared-visible images captured by satellites.  This technique, called FIRe-GAN, generates high-quality, infrared-visible composite images from single multi-spectral images, allowing for the creation of a synthetic dataset.  By training this model on a large dataset using the AdamW optimizer and a least-squares loss function, we achieve state-of-the-art results and demonstrate the efficacy of FIRe-GAN through a range of evaluations.  Furthermore, FIRe-GAN has significant practical applications, offering a versatile tool for disaster responders and trained algorithms to identify wildfires.

While detecting depression using social media indicates, it is vital to deconfound indications' connections to Z (the underlying trait) as the platform's limited view of a person enables only partial insight into Z.  To address this challenge, I assembled a dataset with annotated social media posts, which is now made accessible through a public repository for scrutiny and research.  This dataset comprises 1,000 eye-catching indications gathered from a large corpus, allowing for an examination of the present methods for identifying depression using social media signs.  Through empirical analysis, I investigated the merits and shortcomings of several supreme indications, such as feelings of failure, sorrowful music, and low social connections, and examined how their classification accuracy correlates with their ranking by human validators.  By comparing the performance of cutting-edge techniques using our newly assembled dataset, I highlighted some of the reasons why current methods are not yet sufficient for deconfusing social media signs for predicting depression.

We've developed a stochastic model that uses random compartment techniques to simulate the dynamics of COVID-19 infections in a general population. The model considers factors like demographics, proximity, hygiene practices, and severity of disease outcomes. It also assumes a non-uniform population with different exposure levels and risk of death from the virus. The model's core consists of three primary components: (i) a stochastic routine that creates a demographic population with the specified exposure and mortality characteristics, (ii) a compartment-based infection dynamics model that includes isolation, and (iii) a simulation routine that applies random stress events such as those simulated by Gompertzian growth to the model. These events can trigger larger outbreaks, leading to more severe cases and higher mortality rates. The model uses past data on US mortality rates to simulate scenarios, calculating measures like the cumulative percentage of the population that have died from the virus and average individual infection duration over time. It's shown that the model accurately predicts future mortality rates across different demographic groups when adjustments are made to the model parameters. This includes better performance than naive models that predict future outcomes based only on past trends.

To determine the threshold energy of the isoscalar giant monopole resonance in nuclei, the explicit dependence on a particular interaction type that couples monopole and quadrupole vibrations is investigated. This interaction is known as the tensor forcing and originates from the Pauli principle. It causes a trail-by-light effect and significantly influences the energy of monopole excitations when a significant amount of a particular configuration is involved. To understand this effect, a particular approach involving the restriction of a particular configuration in the quadrupole operator is implemented. It is understood that this limitation induces a rough approximation but is implemented here due to the lack of alternative methodologies. To study the influence of tensor forcing, the isoscalar giant monopole resonance in certain nuclei is analyzed. Evidently, this restriction has a considerable impact on the energy of monopole excitations in nuclei that show a substantial component from a particular configuration. It is understood, however, that this impact is minimal in nuclei that do not show a significant component from a particular configuration. Moreover, this restriction affects not just the energy but also the width of monopole excitations. Experimentally measured widths are used here to verify the reliability of calculated estimates. Finally, despite tensor forcing's considerable impact, it is understood that this effect is relatively minor when compared to other factors that determine the properties of giant resonances.

Systems featuring stick-slip behavior, governed by the principles of friction and driven by an external force, are widespread across both natural and industrial contexts. The dynamic interaction between these forces is often represented by coupled differential equations that account for movement, torque, and stick-point slip. The inclusion of Coulomb friction necessitates consideration of the stick-pose equation in addition to the slip-pose equation. Consequently, the system's behavior becomes dependent on the properties of both the system and the used feedback mechanism. From a theoretical perspective, the system's behavior near an equilibrium point on the attractor can be understood through the means of a linearized model. Notably, the application of certain feedback mechanisms is capable of generating diverse patterns of stick-slip oscillations, which have been observed both in laboratory settings and with the human hand. This is attributed to the emergence of stable attractors associated with these mechanisms. The research presented in this thesis explores a broad scope of stick-slip models, encompassing both one- and two-dimensional systems featuring Coulomb friction. The application of various feedback mechanisms to these models enables a comprehensive analysis, encompassing both the establishment and extinction of stick-slip oscillations, as well as the development of multiple attractors. The research indicates that multiple attractors can form when the system exhibits localized properties distinct from its surroundings. The phenomenon is proven to arise from a codimension-two bifurcation specifically located at the snaking boundary, a critical region where the system's behavior becomes multist

We introduce a novel model, deep Bellman risk management (DBRM), to predict future reward standard deviations based on current states and policy outputs. This approach can optimize the performance of reinforcement learning (RL) agents by limiting their risk exposure during training. Our analysis verifies the convergence of DBRM's policy gradient in a specific context and provides general proof of its feasibility for continuous control tasks. Additionally, we conduct experiments to evaluate DBRM's effectiveness in continuously adjusting its exploration strategy according to varying risk tolerance and confirming its capability to expedite the reduction of training latency by mitigating risk.

In online interaction, users' deliberate intentions often emerge gradually as a result of their interactions.  Currently, most current machine learning approaches for making recommendations ignore users' real goals or treat them as fixed factors.  In reality, understanding and modeling these subjective intentions is a vital component of providing relevant and effective recommendations. This research develops a novel approach to identify and categorize the underlying intentions of users in the context of item sequence recommendations. Different from previous studies, our approach views user intentions as a dynamic component of the system, where new intentions can be discovered at any time and old ones revised based on additional information.  We use a hierarchical network of hidden intentions and define a model for each stage, focusing on the most relevant data when classifying intentions.  We collect and annotate a large dataset from user clicks and implement a dynamic Bayesian network to automate the process of extracting relevant data for users, thereby allowing our approach to adapt to users' ever-changing goals.  We also use a hierarchical Dirichlet model to categorize user intentions, with each level representing progressively broader groups of intentions.  We collected a unique dataset of user clicks on videos and found that users' real goals closely align with existing product category classifications, providing a valuable resource for researchers and the recommendation field in general.

The double confluent Heun equation has been shown to be "small" in the sense of the Sturm theory, and it also forms the initial equation of a symmetric unfolding, referred to as the PCSU, from the "small" equation obtained through a certain deformation. This deformation, specifically a penetration into the "large" region, is unique in the sense that it results in a equation known as the Bessel equation. This particular unfolding, PCSU, is notable due to its "universal" nature, and solutions to the PCSU can be expressed using the hypergeometric series, and as such, properties previously identified for the double confluent Heun equation, such as sign variation, have also been found to apply to the PCSU. Notably, the PCSU is "penetrable" into the "large" region in a singular manner when compared to other unfoldings and this phenomenon is unique to this particular unfolding.

The concept of matrix evaluation with heterogeneous properties, having different subgroups, is introduced and defined as a tensor product of transformation operators acting on intergroup and intragroup features. A fundamental error is identified for this property and a corresponding matrix evaluation is constructed, with its rank determined. When each subgroup has its own set of features, the matrix evaluation reduces to a property with multiple subproperties, and its rank becomes constrained due to dependencies between subproperties. This constraint leads to a fundamental error, and a corresponding matrix evaluation is constructed, with its rank determined. The fundamental errors for matrix evaluations with heterogeneous properties and subproperties are interconnected, and a fundamental error is identified for the final case, consisting of group-wise homogeneous properties with different subproperties.

A crucial category of transformations, devoid of symmetry, serves as the foundation for a comprehensive and all-encompassing topological structure. A novel topological system, referred to as the 'NSS-structure,' is introduced in this paper, emphasizing the distinctive attributes associated with each element. The paper demonstrates that the NSS-structure is a universal framework for representation, incorporating various concepts such as vector fields, curves, and surface normals in the absence of symmetry. Additionally, we show that the NSS-structure provides a unique platform for analyzing a range of ideas recently proposed by T. Y. Tseng, which are published in a series of papers.

We introduce the semi-inclusive LFV ratio $R_{LFV}^{\ell^+\ell^-}$ to study the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transition independently of theoretical uncertainties in hadronic physics, by evaluating the ratio of inclusive and exclusive semileptonic decays of $B\to K(\ell^+\ell^-)\ell^-$. This combined observable is sensitive to multiple Wilson coefficients and may provide insights into the contribution of the $Q_{21}$ coefficient if present, given that it's challenging to determine the $Q_{10}$ coefficient independently. Assuming that $Q_{21}$ doesn't significantly influence $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ decays, we analyze their $R_{LFV}^{\mu^+ \mu^-}$ under the standard model and a specific New Physics scenario involving a dark sector leptoquark, while also considering the advantages and limitations of this combined observable.

We focus on networks of interconnected linear systems, consisting of $m$ channels each containing an $n$-dimensional system, as our primary object of study. The channels communicate through one-way channels. The overall goal is to develop a decentralized, stable regulation method that able to be implemented by all agents, including those in the inner loop, as well as evaluating its connectivity requirements. Leveraging a central observation that achieves detailed system knowledge, we first demonstrate the existence of a specific controller that enables complete, detailed system reproduction. Inspired by the properties of pinning controllability in complex networks, we then explore which subgraph sections of the system's communication network contribute to this reproduction, thereby allowing us to determine the minimum required connectivity within the system's network structure for the proposed regulation method to be applicable. Notably, to ensure reproducibility through a greatly expanded system, we discover that it is only necessary for some system nodes to possess relative primality between their dimensions and the overall system dimension in order for them to contribute to the reproduction, thus presenting a more flexible criterion than before. As a result, we are able to achieve a decentralized, stable regulation method that is capable of being implemented by all agents, as well as a clear, systematic approach for establishing and evaluating the connectivity requirements of the system's network structure. Thispins a novel method for determining the feasibility of implementing a global controller through a selection of sensitive nodes within the system's network, thus offering a more advanced approach than before for

The COVID-19 pandemic has become one of the most severe health crises in recent years,
causing widespread disruption and economic devastation.
As the outbreak has shown no signs of abating, it is essential to develop reliable systems
for detecting the virus at an early stage to prevent its spread and minimize casualties.
The virus-spreading speed can be controlled by predicting whether an infected individual
is likely to transmit the disease to others. Therefore, it is crucial to develop a system
that can accurately classify individuals into two phases, based on their transmission
potential. Building on the capabilities of pre-trained language models like BERT,
researchers have explored the potential of using these models in developing
classification systems that leverage textual information. Despite these efforts, there
has been a lack of studies on using BERT for two-phase classification. In response to
this gap, our team proposes a novel approach to classify individuals into two phases
using textual data, specifically targeting COVID-19 spread prevention. The BERT Attributes
model is trained on attribute data derived from BERT's self-attention mechanism,
creating six unique attributes for each sample. These attributes are then combined to
class a patient into one of two phases.

This introductory guide is designed for network research enthusiasts who want to
explore the core principles of networking and gain a thorough understanding of
the fundamental algorithms and models that drive current research advancements.

Early formulations of eco-evolutionary processes were based on a linear model, where the direct relationship between changes in selection and adaptation led to a predictable, linear change in the mean fitness. However, this linear model was later disproven through theoretical and simulations, revealing a different, non-linear relationship. Despite this revised understanding, the term 'eco-evolutionary dynamics' often implies a range of discrete states, like 'fast', 'intermediate', and'slow', rather than a continuous description. Our goal is to bridge this gap and introduce a framework that allows for both detailed, mechanistic descriptions and broader, qualitative understandings of eco-evolutionary processes. To achieve this, we focus on how different'regulators' control the duration of key phases in the eco-evolutionary process and use existing theories to develop a framework for its characterization. By identifying key parameters, this framework offers a systematic approach for qualitative understanding of eco-evolutionary processes, exemplified through its application to the well-studied models of Abbott's theory of quantitative adaptation and the Snowdrift game.

When using unsupervised speech learning without context, improved speech recognition skills often conflict with other abilities such as understanding speech patterns, as progress in speech recognition can hinder learning other related skills, a phenomenon where progress in one area hampers progress in another, a concept often seen in learning processes, a trend that can also be observed in the efficiency of speech learning models where model size and complexity also plays a crucial role, suggesting that smaller speech models may actually perform better in certain situations, a conclusion that also poses questions on the current best practices in speech learning.

This research explores the emerging trend of Distributed Exchanges (DEXes). Unlike conventional exchanges, DEXes utilize decentralized technology, such as Blockchain and Smart Contracts, to facilitate trading. By redefining the trading landscape, DIXes present opportunities and challenges, including enhanced security, reduced regulatory risk, and improved efficiency. However, DEXes also face limitations in trading volumes, liquidity, and user adoption. Our analysis delves into the key players in the DEX market, examining their strengths and weaknesses, with the aim of identifying potential benchmarks for success. Furthermore, we outlines the crucial technical and regulatory factors that must be addressed to develop effective DEXs. Our investigation culminates in a classification model that helps explain the varying levels of user adoption among different DEXs, with Uniswap being identified as a best practice example. By the end of this research, readers will have a comprehensive understanding of the DEX space, allowing them to become informed participants in the growing decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystem.

Traditional sensitivity analyses focus on uncertainties associated with study parameters, but this study introduces a novel framework that identifies and assesses uncertainties tied to study design or data elements.  Inspired by the concept of the 'E-value', a metric utilized in observational studies to quantify the impact of absent data, this work develops a Bayesian framework that enables assessment of the sensitivity associated with uncollected study data.  Key distinctions between this new framework and others are established, with a comprehensive overview provided of the methodologies employed in 157 recent systematic reviews, revealing a need for such analyses.  A detailed illustration of the proposed method is given using data from the Oslo Study, with results showing its effectiveness in identifying potential sources of uncertainty.  Furthermore, additional examples are offered to illustrate the versatility and applicability of the proposed framework.

The study of the quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q_[x,y]$ begins with a generating function analysis over the polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}_q}[x,y]$. A basis for the extended Laurent expansion of $f\in \mathbb{C}_q}[x,y]$ is established as the set $\mathcal{B}_f$, which consists of words combining $x$, $x^{-1}$, $y$, and $y^{-1}$ in such a way that their degrees are constrained by those of $f$. Further research focuses on the properties of the set $\mathcal{B}_f$. A function $\kappa_f$ is introduced, defining a weight assignment for elements in $\mathcal{B}_f$, which follows a specific U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)-symmetry rule. Each element $b$ of $\mathcal{B}_f$ is characterized by its degree and kernel $N_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)(b)$. Moreover, for a given involution $\mathcal{S}$ over $\mathbb{C}_q)[x,y]$, the set $\mathcal{B}_f^{\mathcal{S}}$ is determined, which satisfies certain U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)-symmetry conditions. In the context of the Internet of Vehicles, a decentralized system of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has significant implications for the educational sector as well. To address the challenges associated with data security and privacy in this area, a robust blockchain-enabled federated learning framework can be employed. This study conducts an in-depth analysis of existing literature to examine solutions for securing IoT data and promoting learning in a vehicle-based setting. Noting the proliferation of vehicular IoT applications, this work focuses primarily on the educational applications of blockchain-enabled federated learning. It systematically evaluates and synthesizes relevant research, paving the way for the development of novel frameworks and platforms in this field.

The LHCb experiment measures the beauty and charm production cross-sections at a 5.02 TeV proton-proton collision energy to validate QCD-based predictions. The results consider both direct and non-prompt D meson production, where non-prompt refers to D mesons containing a b-quark, unlike the prompt, where the b-quark forms a complete B meson. The data used incorporates a large dataset of integrated luminosity, enabling a precise measurement. The beauty and charm results, specifically for semi-muon decay of D mesons, show agreement with established theoretical models. However, experimental data on all D meson production, including semi-leptonically decaying D+، D0، D*+ and D+*-, reveals a significant discrepancy with these models, quantified as 2.5σ, hinting at underlying systematic uncertainties in the measurement process.

Superconducting quantum computing devices require extremely low temperatures to operate. Currently, researchers utilize dilution refrigerators, but there's a lack of reliable experimental data on the thermal history within modern cryogenic systems. To address this, our team is utilizing the ORE A user facility at Fermilab to develop a large (660 mm in diameter by 3000 mm in length) cryostat that maintains temperatures as low as 10 millikelvin. Our paper describes the platform's material selection, design, and testing, achieving a thermal gradient of 0.1 to 3 millikelvin across its length at 10 millikelvin temperatures. This successful demonstration showcases a reliable and modular cryogenic system with documented thermal performance.

In recent years, the adoption of cryptocurrencies has been marked by significant growth, with leading security experts and industry watchers pointing out an alarming gap in current understanding - the extent to which existing knowledge on cryptocurrency-related security risks is being implemented in practice. Our study, the first extensive analysis of security best practices in popular Python cryptocurrency libraries, sheds light on this knowledge gap by examining the degree to which existing best practices are being implemented in real-world Python cryptocurrency projects. Our comprehensive analysis of 15 such projects across 312 code samples reveals disturbingly common violations of accepted security standards, with 70% of the code samples exhibiting at least one security risk and 38% exceeding five such risks. Moreover, our investigation links these security risks to 21 potential hacking techniques, with the primary concern being the potential for a two-stage code execution exploit. Our results highlight the gravity of the existing security threat landscape and underscore the necessity for cross-industry efforts to improve cryptocurrency-related code best practices.

In modern cities, the proliferation of smart devices and sensors generates vast amounts of data, necessitating effective methods for organizing and searching the information. A key application of information organization in this context is radio-based tag detection, used to pinpoint locations within city maps by analyzing signals from mobile devices or satellite constellations. Existing methods, relying on cell tower data or satellite signals, are limited to specific environments and face challenges such as intermittent signal loss, baseline shifting, and obstructions. To address these issues, we developed WORTH, a real-time, open framework leveraging citywide wireless signals to accurately determine users' locations on urban maps. By combining urban wireless data analysis with machine learning algorithms, WORTH can pinpoint locations with high precision, even in environments with limited or missing wireless data. Our framework consists of a wireless sensing module for gathering relevant data, a geographical module for collecting urban information, and an analysis module integrating machine learning algorithms to calculate the best possible location. As proof of concept, we created a fictional city and demonstrated WORTH's effectiveness using simulated data, showcasing its versatility and integrity.

We introduce a new deep learning model called the Nonuniform Sparse Model, which is based on the elementary convolutional operator and the Pseudo Hough Distance. This model effectively interprets the nonuniform sparse pattern as a non-linear geometric transformation and is capable of being transformed into various sparse models through different transformations. We propose the NuSPAN, a novel Pseudo Hough Deep Architecture, which utilizes a two-branch network structure to respectively identify geometric key points and their corresponding transformations. Each branch is composed of multiple residual layers to fulfill the objective and perform a forward transformation to recover the sparse representation. We test the effectiveness of NuSPAN on synthetic and real seismic data and demonstrate its ability to accurately recover the sparse representation and achieve better inversion results than traditional MUltipurpose Seismic Inversion with Artificial Neural Networks.

This article investigates semigroups of linear operators within the context of BMOA-type harmonic blanket spaces. By establishing two key definitions, we delve into the generation of semigroups via bounded linear operators acting on specific Banach lattices, and we explore the connection between these operators and integral transforms, particularly the Darwin-Newtonian type operators. Subsequently, we derive several significant theorems that highlight the critical roles of growth conditions in our operators.

A recently developed method links wavefunction overlaps to an operator algebra based on amenable construction. In the present study, we specifically demonstrate how to obtain amenable corrections for Haagerup model wavefunctions, which were previously expressed as matrix elements within a specific model of linearly-dependent quantum states. By applying the operator algebra method, we identify a subalgebra corresponding to the original model and a larger algebra representing an overlapped version. The overlapped version incorporates sum-over-states inputs, which can be mapped to a new, higher-dimensional algebra. Specifically, for Haagerup model wavefunctions, which exhibit finite-length corrections, we show that the overlapped version's additivity in length can be attributed to an amenable correction, determined by a specific density matrix. Moreover, we show that the diagonal elements of an important positive operator - which was previously noted to be non-diagonal within the original model - exhibit linear, long-length approximations that are entirely determined by the finite-length corrections for specific model states.

Accurate part-of-speech classification of ancient texts necessitates a solid alignment with the correct syntax and grammar structure, as any misclassification would result in a distorted understanding of the text's meaning and origin. Despite the reliance on 18th-century grammatical rules, early automated tagging methods proved ineffective, while modern machine-learning approaches have tended to oversimplify the tagging process by applying a single, uniform rule to all texts, regardless of their date or origin. This inflexible strategy has led to considerable constraints on analyzing ancient texts using automated tools. A breakthrough in this field comes from leveraging the power of deep learning and set-valued functions to improve the accuracy of ancient text part-of-speech classification, a feature absent from discussions on applying NLP to historical collections.

This research paper explores a broad category of nonsmooth functions, which we believe can be handled by an integrability principle similar to the Sylvester constraint, traditionally applied to smooth functions. We also establish a new criterion for smooth functions, which must meet a weak constraint in order to apply the principle. Our findings extend to the analysis of a nonsmooth variant of the polynomial Saint-Pierre conjecture recently proposed by the fourth author.

The proliferation of smart city platforms and devices, including mobile devices and digital assistants like Siri and Alexa, has made it easier for citizens to interact with urban infrastructure. Interaction designs, whether physical or virtual, are initially conceived as conceptual models before being translated into technical specifications. Unfortunately, these interaction concepts often lack concrete representation and are mainly understood through their subjective application. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that uses a formal specification to detail the structure of conversation and the expected user responses in order to enhance the effectiveness of voice assistants. By combining this approach with a digital assistant's built-in language processing capabilities, we can refine the assistant's functionality by: 1) capturing user interactions through natural language and reinterpreting them according to a standardized conceptual model, 2) formally defining the structure of the resulting conversation and the expected user responses, and 3) translating the interaction into technical specifications suitable for implementation. We utilised a systematic mapping approach to translate the conceptual model into a formal specification and tested its usability in a real-world context. By representing the expectation of a smart assistant's functionality in a standardized formal format, we can reimagine the role of digital assistants as facilitators of more rational design processes.

A new method, concealed inverses protocol (CIP), utilizes ungated qubit inverses to tackle stochastic errors in quantum computations. Here, the CIP implementation on a given circuit is compared to classic quantum error correction techniques via simulation using a established noise model based on superconducting quantum systems. Our results indicate that the CIP prevents error escalation from subsequent gates once an error occurs, whereas other correction methods hinder the computation's efficiency. Additionally, the CIP shows compatibility with a variety of calculations, including those requiring multiple gate sequences.

In a general category denoted as $\mathbb{C}$ with arbitrary limits present, we define a concept of "preorder-like structure" within the category framework. This is achieved through a subcategory of relations in $\mathbb{C}$, where the defined relations respect equality, creating a preordinal subcategory. In this setting, we establish a duality, where a preordinal subcategory corresponds to a subcategory equipped with an equivalence connection that is expressively equivalent to the original category. Additionally, we define a concept of "depiction relation" as a specific equivalence relation in $\mathbb{C}$, indicating that a certain category $\mathbb{D}$, which is equivalent to $\mathbb{C}$, is a valid depiction of $\mathbb{C}$ if every preorder-like structure in $\mathbb{C}$ can be isomorphically mapped to $\mathbb{D}$, with depiction relations satisfying this condition being in relative abundance.

To study extreme sea levels and their correlation with wind and waves at various ports, we utilize a multivariate spatial model. This approach accounts for the seasonal variation in sea level fluctuations and their dependence on local wind and waves. Based on 218 years of data from six marine environments, our analysis reveals that coastal storms cause elevated sea levels, and we observe a positive connection between wind and waves and sea level peaks. This relationship is especially pronounced in regions with intense wind and waves. Our findings are further validated by simulating future extreme sea levels using a resampling technique.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by significant semantic gaps between images and texts during the initial training phase. To address this challenge, we present a new approach that integrates Exemplar Contrastive Learning to tighten image-text correlations. Notably, our technique enables the efficient utilization of ordinary daily examples with supplementary visual information, thereby overcoming the constraint of costly, domain-specific datasets. Subsequently, we achieve state-of-the-art results on multiple Visual Retrieval tasks and conduct a thorough analysis to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed VT-CLIP model.

The task of accurately solving a noisy matrix system is crucial and extremely common in scientific research, found extensively in fields such as magnetic resonance imaging, computer vision, and other image processing disciplines, as well as finite element analysis and other computational methods that involve large data sets. Although a particular method, universal Krylov iterative methods, has been widely used for this purpose, it has been found that such generic approaches may not be the most effective for specific applications. In our study, we take a different approach by developing a novel, flexible algorithm that enables efficient, precise solution of a wide range of noisy matrix systems by breaking down the problem into a series of basic systems. This innovative technique enables the construction of new iterative methods, such as the QRSS method, that outperform traditional Krylov methods, including the widely-used CG method, in particular, by showing a significant reduction in average iteration count by at least one order of magnitude for specific applications, including the finite element analysis of a realistic brain MRI case, and other tested methods. Furthermore, we extend our approach by designing a new family of iterative methods, such as the QRSS-CG family, that not only demonstrate comparable or even improved convergence rates but, more importantly, exhibit increased iteration efficiency and flexibility, thus making them more adaptable to matrix structures than their predecessors.

We explicitly identify and categorize the segments of quaternionic spectral categories, which are a type of quaternionic generalization of Eilenberg-Mac Lane categories. These spectral categories are essentially one-dimensional quaternionic parametrized spaces. Building upon the Segal formalism, we develop a homotopy-categorical analogue for quaternionic spectral categories, producing a defined 2-category. Next, we establish a connection to quaternionic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra by categorifying the segments of quaternionic spectral categories, ultimately contributing to the study of functor calculus in categories enriched in the category of quaternionic spectra.

Given a k-dimensional local Noetherian ring A with a field k as a quotient, we can form the generic coordinate ring of a configuration of k points as a quotient of the polynomial ring k[x_1,...,x_k]. The F-rational closure of a local ring A, denoted R_{+m}^F, is the largest subring consisting of elements m times as potent as those in the original ring. The F-rational closure of a local Noetherian ring is itself Noetherian. The paper demonstrates that if a local Noetherian ring A meets a certain condition - it is locally F-regular and has a certain coordinate degree - the Hilbert function of the quotient ring constructed from a configuration of points over the field k is equal to its lowest degree polynomial across a certain range. The authors also provide alternative interpretations of this finding, as well as a related standard degree conjecture regarding the dimension of the ring's quotient, a hypothesis supported by recent studies.

The application of machine learning in human disease diagnosis is at an inflection point, 
with significant progress being made in evaluating imaging-based models using 
archived data. Nonetheless, there is no unified standard for training models with 
image annotations and clinical data across different institutions and countries. 
This lack of standardization has caused issues with data interoperability, 
compounding the challenge of bringing machine learning into clinical practice. 
Solutions to these problems involve developing high-level workflows for data 
annotation, model training, and post-hoc analysis to optimize performance, and 
using metadata to facilitate data manipulation and visualization. The DICOM standard 
provides a comprehensive approach to storing and communicating medical imaging data, 
and our Python framework, highdicom, offers a way to integrate these standards into 
the workflow of researchers and clinicians. By incorporating the DICOM standard, 
highdicom enables the creation of compatible files containing image annotations and 
model predictions, facilitating the sharing and verification of model results across 
the medical imaging community. 

Highdicom is released under the highly permissive MIT license and is hosted on 
PyPI. The package includes a comprehensive documentation site and source code, 
and our study demonstrates its capabilities by sharing pathology-centric image 
annotations and model predictions in accordance with the DICOM standard using 
Highdicom. 

Highdicom expands upon the pathology-centric toolkit, GR idiPath, and our study 
demonstrates its first successful use in generating a DICOM

We analyze a double-field generalization of Einstein-Hilbert action and derive its surface energy-momentum tensor by employing the Palais theorem, which enables the extension of Noether construction to a scalar configuration space. The resulting surface expression of Einstein-Hilbert action respects the Palais slice condition. As a consequence, we establish that the surface energy-momentum tensor is equivalent to the 3D Einstein-Hilbert action's Noether charge. As a byproduct of this equivalence, we show that the 2009 CKS entropy formula is inherently tied to the 3D surface energy-momentum tensor. Additionally, the central charge of the resulting Virasoro algebra, produced from the double-field generalization of Einstein-Hilbert action, is equivalent to the CKS entropy.

In the rapidly expanding field of genomic big data, effective embedding of genomic sequences is essential to convert complex genetic information into simple, easy-to-interpret vectors. Current sequence encoding methods primarily root their methods in existing knowledge about protein structures that have been well-studied. By contrast, a novel supervised approach has been developed to uncover the inherent patterns inherent to DNA sequences from scratch. Additionally, a comprehensive dataset has been created to benchmark the effectiveness of this approach. The results demonstrate that this method is capable of producing high-quality embeddings that capture underlying DNA sequence characteristics successfully. Furthermore, it has been discovered that a substantial portion of embedded features can be explained by known genetic factors influencing disease susceptibility, which also shows that many of these factors are interconnected in a complex network. With its ability to uncover explainable features, this method holds significant potential to lead to a better comprehension of the underlying genetics.

The surface modification effect on the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films was investigated by preparing and evaluating a series of epitaxial films on (111) TaN, (0001) Al$_2$O$_3$, and (0001) ZnO substrates. These films, all with a monolayer thickness, exhibited different modes of surface termination: TaN's semimetallic termination, Al$_2$O$_3$’s anisotropic termination due to larger lattice mismatch in the [11$\bar{2}$0] direction, and ZnO’s metallic termination due to smaller lattice mismatch in the [11$\bar{1}$0] direction. Moreover, our findings suggest that the surface termination has no impact on the crystal structure of the films as evidenced by in-plane lattice parameters, however, our results also reveal a significant correlation between the spin-polarization and lattice parameter of the films, which may indicate that the crystal structure has been maintained at a relatively large scale in these films.

We investigate the application of the Clebsch variable technique to three distinct types of Lie-Poisson equations: those associated with Nijenhuis, symplectic, and Lax pairs. We're given the underlying vector field and the associated Poisson structure in the form of a Lie algebra, but the Hamiltonian form is unknown. The technique of the Clebsch map allows us to express unknown variables in terms of new variables with a simple Hamiltonian flow. We demonstrate that the Nijenhuis equation is equivalent to a new equation involving the first variations of new variables. As a consequence, we find that the new variables follow a conserved Hamiltonian flow when the original variables do. We use this approach to simplify the application of Lie-Poisson equations in geometric statistics. We find that the transformation to Clebsch variables for specific Lie algebras can be generalized to the corresponding Gelfand-Cartan pairs. Furthermore, we generalize the Clebsch variable technique to include differential invariants for homogeneous manifolds. We apply this technique to four simple Lie algebras: A1, A2, B1, and G2. Finally, we use Clebsch variables to express Hamiltonians in terms of the invariants of SO(3) and its generalization, U(q)(2), but we're given the invariants, not the Hamiltonian. The technique of the Clebsch map allows us to express unknown Hamiltonians in terms of new variables

In our study of the KMTNet Anomaly Project's sub-prime field, we analyzed microlensing planetary anomalies from 2018, identifying 12 occurrences out of 34 total planets observed in this dataset. By examining these anomalies, we were able to identify all relevant relevant information related to observed events, including detailed maps of the lensing system and associated systematic effects. These findings reveal that a significant majority of low-mass-ratio planets exhibit non-uniform dimming in relation to systematic errors, according to a new test. Furthermore, we discovered that a symmetrical model of the lensing system fails to adequately describe 11 out of 12 observed events, ultimately pointing to the presence of a third unresolvable body that impedes the understanding of the lensing phenomenon. These unique characteristics can only be fully explained by employing a more advanced model, such as a single-mass lens with an associated secondary body. Consequently, we propose that a substantial proportion of low-mass-ratio planets may possess this complex structure, with a possible rate of occurrence that could significantly impact the overall population study. Additionally, we use our Anomaly Project's comprehensive data to test and validate the planet-mass-relationship theory proposed by Adachi et al. 2020. A thorough examination of our Anomaly Project's findings supports the theory's validity, suggesting that a substantial discrepancy actually exists in the planet-mass-relationships observed in the KMTNet-2018 Prime Field, as previously documented

This is the second paper in a series that focuses on the development of a novel mathematical framework for conserving quantities in fluid dynamics and associated physical laws. This paper specifically examines the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, while the first paper looked at incompressible fluids. It discusses the challenges posed by quantity conservation when a fluid's state changes from being compressible to incompressible or vice versa. Additionally, it highlights issues that arise from a particular mathematical representation called entropy, especially when a fluid's density approaches zero. The conservation principles in fluid dynamics, particularly for energy and momentum, are reviewed and analyzed for both compressible and incompressible flows.

This paper evaluates 20 classification machine learning models for their performance in predicting protein domains from protein sequences and uses the Uniprot protein sequence dataset.  The paper initially provides an overview of the protein domain prediction problem, before highlighting its significance in present day biomedical research.  Three distinct features are extracted from the dataset and their effect on model performance is analyzed using a feature importance assessment method.  The paper concludes by comparing the performance of different machine learning models and discusses the outcomes.

We define a variant of fundamental symmetric functions, $\lambda\mapsto \tilde{\Lambda}_q(\lambda)$, in terms of $q$-Pochhammer symbols and relate this to $q$-rook theory on Dyck trails, also establishing an equivalence with modified fundamental $\lambda$-homogeneous symmetric functions, $\tilde{\Lambda}_q(\lambda) \simeq H_q(\lambda)$. Additionally, we study the combinatorial properties of $\Lambda_{q}^{(m)}(\lambda)$, which represents the sum of various $q$-extended Kostka numbers, found in a study by Gutfreund and Matsumoto.

The performance of convolutional neural networks largely depends on the spatial arrangement of input data. This fact motivated the exploration of conventional networks that utilize both horizontal and vertical convolutions to capture image patterns in diverse orientations. Our research shows that incorporating orientation convolutions leads to significant improvements in classification tasks, particularly for images containing patterns or artifacts in both horizontal and vertical directions. Notably, this advancement was demonstrated on several benchmark tests, such as identifying handwritten characters and estimating age from facial features.

A new type of algebraic object called a curved Curry equation is proposed, which takes inspiration from the curved equations of differential geometry. The curved Curry equation serves as a generalized form of the traditional trace equation. By utilizing Curry equations, various solutions can be generated for the original trace equation under specific constraints. The potential of using curved equations to create a comprehensive theory of 'extreme values' is also explored, drawing from the foundations of mathematical economics and mathematical logic. In addition, an innovative method for solving linear equations is developed, which relies on the concept of a'reference line'. The proposed approach offers practical applications, as demonstrated through a novel solution to the problem of finding the reference line for a standard linear equation under given constraints. The resulting solution not only involves calculating the equation but also determining the optimal reference line for Curry equations, creating a new paradigm for solving traditional linear equations. Furthermore, the approach highlights the distinct characteristics of solving curved and non-curved equations. By incorporating the concept of a'reference line,' the traditional problem of finding the solution to an linear equation is reinterpreted as a geometric issue, much like a problem involving finding tangent lines on a surface in differential geometry.

In hadronic collisions, the average mass of top quarks created in proton-proton collisions solely depends on the transverse momentum (pT) of the top quarks and the center-of-mass energy, regardless of any pT-dependent flavor asymmetry that might exist. Although this asymmetry vanishes at Born level, it does influence the pT distribution through the radiative corrections generated by the weak color force. However, since the subleading terms fade rapidly with increasing pT, the prominent flavor distortion is pronounced at intermediate pT values but diminishes at high pT values. Therefore, if data are analyzed over a broad pT range or when statistics improve, the flavor asymmetry's effect on the top quark mass measurement becomes negligible, and our finding implies that the measured mass differs little, if at all, from the true mass, independent of any assumptions about the asymmetry's origin.

We examine an instance of graph tinting where vertices are assigned a specific color in a particular pattern. Specifically, we look at instances on a subset of vertices from a near-regular graph, with each vertex colored in a unique way, and an additional constraint: adjacent vertices must be colored in a sequence. Our goal is to develop a theory for a subset of these instances, which we call "effective triples." By studying these instances, we can prove a subset of them have a resolution bounded by a specific, relatively small number. This finding has further implications on how these instances can be solved, and we can prove a subset of these have a solution that can be found through a relatively simple method.

We show that a hypercontractive inequality holds for certain subspaces of scaled Bergman spaces over the unit disk, with the possibility of sharpness depending on the value of $\alpha$ and the nature of the exponent $p$. This finding settles an open issue first introduced by Lieb and Loss's book.

The pandemic caused by the COVID-19 virus has become a global health threat, with the World Health Organization listing it as a Public Health Emergency of International Concern since March 2020. To combat this, researchers have been conducting extensive epidemiological studies on the disease to inform public policy and healthcare systems, while also developing treatments and a vaccine. Groundbreaking medical AI systems have significantly aided virus diagnosis, treatment, and prevention, drawing the attention of scientific communities worldwide. Although these developments have been impressive, there is still room for improvement in creating reliable detection systems, especially those using deep learning techniques. To contribute positively, this paper presents a method for detecting COVID-19 using low-dose computed tomography scans, an essential procedure in diagnosing the disease. Utilizing a massive dataset of 14,052 double-blinded images, the researchers have created an advanced detection method that outperforms current standards, especially in terms of detecting non-COVID-19 cases. Through extensive experiments, the proposed algorithm has shown exceptional performance, achieving an impressive 93.54% accuracy and 86.52% accuracy for COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 detection, respectively. What's more, the proposed method has proven to be robust and efficient, even when detecting images with noise and other distortions. This breakthrough is significant because it marks the first time a capsule network has been used to create a diagnostic system for detecting COVID-19, making it a pioneering work in the field.

In recent years, there has been an extraordinary surge in the number of artificial objects in Low-Earth Orbit, with the total number surpassing 8,000 objects. Historically, the primary concern for space missions was avoiding collisions with existing debris in the area, but with the increased objects in orbit, the problem has shifted to managing the spatial distribution of these objects. This shift is necessitated by the diminished timeframe to react to situations, as well as the increased likelihood of encounters with other objects in orbit. The objective of this research is to explore strategies for optimizing spatial usage in Low-Earth Orbit by analyzing mission spatial requirements and suggesting methods to reduce the integration of new missions into existing configurations, thus maximizing spatial efficiency. By achieving this, the likelihood of orbits that are vulnerable to collisions and perturbations can be minimized, resulting in significant cost savings and increased flexibility for future missions in Low-Earth Orbit.

Recent advances in optimization-based mesh generation have yielded efficient methods for producing meshes with optimal properties. In our research, we employ whole number linear optimization to create coarsely structured quadrilateral meshes on 2D CAD point sets. By casting mesh generation as an optimization problem that involves generating new vertices, we define constraints that ensure resulting meshes comprise quadrilaterals and adhere to original design specifications. Whole number solutions enable the use of off-the-shelf optimization software to generate meshes suitable for numerical simulation, particularly in finite element methods. Notably, our optimization-based approach prioritizes vertex coarsening, similar to the structure of meshes created through classical mesh improvement methods. Furthermore, we define an objective function that favors vertex coarsening in conjunction with optimal element orientation and gradient orientation. In order to ensure whole number solutions, we restrict vertex positions to the Delaunay mesh, resulting in meshes with optimal coarseness. We compare the quality of meshes produced by our approach with state-of-the-art algorithms in the field.

To assess how well two sets of data align, the sample correlation coefficient can be calculated. Like other sample correlation measures, it's based on arrangements of data and serves as a basis for constructing statistical tests and evaluating random number generators. To develop this measure, the sample correlation coefficient is calculated using two sets of data. At first glance, calculating this measure involves a complex step: determining various moments of a distribution that take into account the interdependence of data. Although general formulas for these moments exist, they were not provided in my previous research. To address this, this study introduces analytical formulas for these moments, making calculations faster and more accurate. These formulas were tested using two sets of data and shown to produce highly accurate results. The time it takes to compute them has been significantly reduced.

We detail the scattering matrix formulation of the force between two objects in a spacetime of any dimensionality, which is valid across any metric setup. Subsequently, it is demonstrated how this method can be employed in both quantum gravity and extra dimensions. Additionally, it is noted how the scattering matrix approach facilitates generalizing gravity and the Yang--Mills theory.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations for incompressible fluids defined on a bounded domain $O$ within $\R^d$, where $d$ equals either three or five. This model incorporates a force $F$ that is both smooth and relatively bounded. Let $S^{l}$ denote the set of all finite dimensional subspaces of smooth functions in $O$. In this research, we establish that for any integer $m$ greater than or equal to one and for any exponent $q$ in the interval from two to infinity, we derive a weak solution for the associated initial boundary value problem under specific boundary conditions when the space $W^{k, q}(O)$, for the exponent $k$ greater than or equal to one plus the difference between $d$ and one, and the space $L^q(0, T; W^{k, q}(O))$, where the interval $[0, T]$ denotes time, are concerned. This problem is approached by the extension of Strichartz estimates in context. Utilizing a generalized version of the Leibitzky division theorem, we break down the space $L^q(0, T; H^1(O))$ in a suitable way, which in turn enables us to prove the desired uniform stabilization. This stabilization results from a finite dimensional localized feedback regulation in the sense of a generalized version of the Kawano-Mabuchi theorem. Consequently, we are able to prove

The development of computational linguistics relies heavily on general knowledge datasets, yet most existing datasets are isolated and cannot be updated after release. To address this issue, we have created a web-based dictionary called LitMind that is dynamically connected to MindMap, a knowledge graph. With over 300 million unique concepts and 1 billion descriptive phrases, LitMind allows for seamless online querying that can be easily integrated into future linguistics systems, making it an irreplaceable resource. Currently, LitMind is accessible through its website and GitHub page, where it also serves as a knowledge foundation for numerous open-source linguistics projects.

Users' diverse backgrounds, expertise, and cultural background lead to varying interpretation abilities when analyzing recommendations. For instance, individuals with limited music knowledge may interpret high-rated albums as 'popular' rather than 'good quality,' while music enthusiasts might judge them based on specific genres or moods. To address this, a new model has been developed that integrates energy-based and generative explanations. LIME-RS is an official implementation of the LIME model for the Ring hierarchical item recommendation system, providing non-linear, local explanations for user interactions. However, as a first attempt at integrating these two approaches, LIME-RS requires improvement in terms of compliance and stability. To rectify this, an analysis was conducted on 149 real-valued features from two music datasets, real-world user interactions were collected and analyzed, and the performance of LIME-RS was assessed using multiple quality metrics. By demonstrating that LIME-RS can enhance human understanding into recommendation models and the nature of user interactions, the model has the potential to enhance interpretation capabilities for recommendation systems.

We investigated the electronic characteristics of the near-surface InAs/GaAs system, focusing on the dependence of the energy gap on hydrostatic pressure for different samples. Our goal was to understand the influence of surface fixed charges on the Fermi level and induce a miniclinic quantum well at the very surface of the sample. Through the application of high-pressure techniques via a diamond anvil cell, both experimental and theoretical evaluations were carried out. The results showed that the surface fixed charges actually originate from the incorporation of arsenic vacancies. The availability of core-level XPS data confirmed that the surface fixed charges can be eliminated through the incorporation of arsenic adlayers. The additional pressure led to the miniclinic quantum well at the very surface of the sample being transformed into a supermicronew quantum well, situated about 5 nanometers from the surface. The observed changes aligned with theoretical predictions from the band structure calculations.

In deep neural networks, regional queries with weighted average pooling (RWAP) have
proven to enhance learning resilience and reduce the impact of adversarial alterations.
However, its effectiveness largely depends on the chosen regional masks, which are often
determined heuristically, leading to inconsistent results. To address this, our research
investigates how different mask design methods affect regional queries' ability to
improve resilience. We specifically examine the advantages of hierarchical division,
non-hierarchical distribution, and random clustering techniques in regional masks.
Through our analysis, we demonstrate the benefits and drawbacks of each method and
how they influence regional queries. Furthermore, we test the efficacy of these methods
in a real-world scenario and compare their performance across various adversarial attacks.

Our previous research, Detailed Account of Sinkhorn (2021), thoroughly explored the Hungarian algorithm, revealing an optimal solution in a specific structure for a subproblem in the Sinkhorn algorithm. This study further analyzes the problem and presents an innovative solution with a time complexity of O(n^2), significantly improved from the original O(n^3) in our previous paper. The novel solution is built upon a unique structure, the collinear triangular array, and a precise kernel function, which enables efficient computations. The time saving can be substantial, especially when the problem has a large size, as it reduces the computational cost of the Sinkhorn algorithm by a factor of n in one of its key subroutines.

AU Mic, a young stellar object approximately 78 million years old, has been observed to have intense star outbursts, which have been studied thoroughly by the NuSTAR and Chandra space telescopes. Past observations by the NuSTAR and FERMI-GBM revealed that the outbursts of this star are characterized by a long, flat high-energy spectrum and an extremely rapid decline in low-energy X-ray emissions. Contrary to these previous findings, our current study discovered a previously unseen X-ray emission pattern during a quiescent period of AU Mic, which was however not present in another quiescent observation made by the NuSTAR. This new observation demonstrated that the outbursts of AU Mic, a young stellar object, start with an extremely low-density hot gas before reaching temperatures of 15 million Kelvin. Our current study also shows that AU Mic's star b and c, which are exoplanets, have stable orbits due to specific orbital characteristics, which ultimately result in stable planetary orbits. Our scientific investigation of AU Mic's quiescent and eruption behavior will serve as a benchmark for future study of other low mass stars.

When high-speed particles hit a resistive substance, it slows them down in a specific manner.  By studying the slowdown, researchers find that there are two distinct effects at work.  The primary effect is a straightforward drag-like force.  In addition, there's a lesser but intriguing phenomenon where the slowdown appears to be connected to the energy lost by the particles.  By accounting for core magnetism in the substance, researchers are able to explain this secondary effect.  The note provides an initial analysis of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) environment using an simplified approach.

The accuracy of distance-based classification methods, such as the ones employed in k-Nearest-Neighbors and k-Nearest-Neighbors bagging algorithms, can be significantly affected by uneven data distribution, resulting in poorly bounded classification errors. In order to enhance these methods' performance in unbalanced spaces, we have developed an alternative method utilizing a localized version of closest neighbor classification. The proposed method adjusts the weight of each region according to its density and starts predicting from the area with the lowest density, potentially reducing the negative impacts of uneven data distribution. A novel, simple algorithm is introduced to balance the weights of diverse regions and associated boundary distances. A comparison of the proposed method with other closest neighbor classification techniques is conducted through simulated data and real-world time-series scenarios.

We have conducted further investigations into a dataset of 67 ultra-bright, very distant quasars that have been collected as part of a ongoing research, combining SkyMapper optical observations with Gaia photometric data. These new discoveries, particularly those that are extremely luminous and reside in the early universe ($z \geq 5.2$), are key findings that help us establish a comprehensive picture of how the universe's massive central black holes grew and developed over time. By using Monte Carlo simulations to account for our survey's full sample of 115 quasars that are as bright as 16th magnitude, we have mapped out with good precision the peak of their luminosity distribution at specific points in the past, such as $z = 6.7$ for when their mass is still growing rapidly and also at $z = 8.4$ for when their mass is in an early stage of development. Our study reveals that in the distant, very luminous end of their spectrum there is very little change in their brightness over time, suggesting a trend that is consistent with their central black holes' rapid mass growth. Our analysis also confirms that very luminous quasars are extremely rare and rapidly changing objects at very distant times and distances from us. These findings help to create a more complete picture of how the central black holes of galaxies in the early universe developed over time.

Measurements taken out of sequence with simulations suggest that charge tunneling between a quantum point and a superconducting island within a hybrid device generates unique electrical signatures. These signatures, resulting from single quasiparticle tunneling, demonstrate nonrandom and correlated variations in current flow. Simulations indicate that random fluctuations in environmental noise cause these signatures, which serve as an early warning system for collaborative heat or charge exchange between the quantum system and the superconducting island.

Results on the convergence of solutions of hyperbolic systems of conservation laws with non-convex flux functions, when initialized with close values, are unified into a single framework. This standards-based approach enables the application of existing convergence criteria, previously tied to specific methods like the Oleinik chain rule, to be now valid for broader classes of flux functions, including those with mixed or distinct convexity properties. Furthermore, the standards approach simplifies the integration of new criteria, such as Lp estimates, by objectifying the underlying convergence protocols.

One significant issue in view synthesis research stems from the non-rigid nature of most real-world scenes, which complicates the creation of new views using solely syntactic view generation techniques. To address this challenge, we present DiffDreamer, a novel approach for single-view new view prediction. Our method employs a conditional diffusion model that integrates cut-style training and multi-scale hierarchical representation techniques to enhance its stability and versatility. Compared to existing conditional diffusion models, our approach offers improved training robustness and generalization capabilities. Experimental evaluations on McQueen and DeepView benchmarks demonstrate DiffDreamer's superiority in terms of overall performance and stability.

Epidemic outbreaks have the potential to cause immense suffering and economic devastation. Early detection and intervention can significantly reduce these consequences if treatment and isolation protocols are swiftly implemented. Predicting the trajectory of an emerging epidemic is crucial for a swift and targeted response. Many models have been developed to forecast infectious disease trends. However, existing predictive frameworks often struggle to adapt to the rapidly changing dynamics of an emerging outbreak, requiring fundamental changes in behavior to prevent overwhelming healthcare systems. We've developed a novel, adaptive forecasting framework that utilizes real-time data to anticipate the trajectory of an emerging epidemic in highly connected systems. By leveraging established metrics, this framework constructs an dynamic prediction pattern that accounts for evolving viral or disease dynamics. Furthermore, this framework enables real-time adjustments to be made to the pattern as new data becomes available, allowing for seamless forecasting even in the absence of timely information.
