We demonstrated the effectiveness of our model by applying it to a simple networked model (the SIS epidemic model) and showed its ability to forecast, update, and stabilize complex dynamics. This framework is versatile and can be applied to various systems, such as air quality, power, transportation, and mobility networks, to predict and regulate system trends.

The stability of a liquid layer surrounding a fiber is examined, with specific focus on the scenario where the liquid is in contact with the fiber surface. This is referred to as the slip boundary condition. Contrary to the scenario where the liquid adheres to the fiber, our results indicate that under the slip condition, the onset of instability occurs at a lower velocity of the fluid and is characterized by a specific type of disturbance. This disturbance in the liquid layer, which forms bubbles, is driven by the phenomenon of Reynolds stress and is influenced by the thickness of the liquid. Our computational model not only explains how the liquid layer becomes unstable under the slip condition, but also reveals a new mechanism of droplet formation that is fueled by the movement of the liquid. This droplet formation mechanism is absent in the scenario where the liquid adheres to the fiber and is instead governed by the movement of the liquid, which generates a pressure imbalance.

The author demonstrates that the solution to the Hunter-Saxton equation is more resistant to perturbations than solutions to the regularized Hunter-Saxton equation. Specifically, if the solution to the regularized equation has a Lipschitz constant of C, then the solution to the original equation has a Lipschitz constant of at most 2C. Building on Panchenko and Voss's findings, this result implies that solutions to certain generalized equations with non-linear terms are also more resistant to perturbations.

The traditional method for detecting scoliosis using ultrasound imaging has limitations in terms of speed and accuracy due to the need for manual scanning by a trained operator. To address this issue, a machine-based ultrasound system is investigated to assess its reliability in detecting scoliosis of the spine. Scoliosis is a spinal condition characterized by abnormal lateral curvature, and accurate, rapid diagnosis is crucial for effective treatment. To evaluate the effectiveness of the new ultrasound system, a study tested its ability to measure coronal spine deformity using the Cobb angle measurement, comparing results with those from manual scans. Two experienced radiologists evaluated the coronal deformity using both manual and robotic scans. Scoliosis instances and Cobb angle measurements were recorded for 30 patients undergoing MRI for unknown spinal issues. Results showed that robotic scanning was as effective as manual scanning in detecting scoliosis (100% agreement) and yielded similar Cobb angle measurements (showing high agreement between the two methods). To further minimize discrepancies, image data from both methods were combined and re-evaluated, achieving excellent levels of agreement for coronal deformity assessments. This study demonstrates the effectiveness and reliability of a robotic ultrasound imaging system in detecting scoliosis, a condition that could reduce treatment costs and improve outcomes by facilitating early interventions. Such an approach also offers new opportunities for the early identification of spinal conditions in individuals with at-risk genetic syndromes or those displaying vague, non-specific spinal symptoms.

The development of spoken language technologies poses difficulties in implementing language models that accurately capture the natural fluctuations in speech utterance lengths. Existing research has explored methods to modify neural language models, such as subword and word-based approaches, to accommodate varying speech lengths. Nevertheless, a significant challenge arises in matching the median length of these modified models with the median length of human speech. We address this issue by proposing an innovative method to create synthetic speech lengths, characterized by a pronounced peak in the length distributions at the median value and gradually decreasing on either side. We compare the efficacy of two distinct length generation techniques - a numerical method proposed by Zemlyak et al. and our own median-driven approach - using models trained on Russian speech. The results demonstrate that our median-driven approach significantly improves the length distribution's proximity to a genuine human speech length distribution. Consequently, we recommend utilizing this median-driven approach for creating length distributions with a distinct mode at or near the median value.

This research explores the utilization of Hate Speech Datasets to train and test a novel approach for detecting hate speech on social media, which outperforms current methods. To counter online hate speech, a different model was developed that focuses on the language's inherent characteristics instead of semantic meaning. The model uses a neural network-based system with two distinct components: one that interprets text through word representations and another that learns the inherent features of hate speech. These two parts combine their outputs through multiplication to identify hate speech. During testing, the model's performance was evaluated on two datasets - one collected from Twitter in 2017 and another from Instagram in 2020 - each labeled as hate speech or not. The results showed that this model outperforms other hate speech detection models, achieving an accuracy of 0.84 or 0.83, depending on the dataset used.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) deep neural network frameworks hold great promise in accelerating the deployment of explainable AI, due to their capability in decomposing deep neural network models into multiple distinct submodels corresponding to individual input features. However, in the context of visual feature extraction, the MIMO framework often produces feature exchanges that are merely correlated with the original inputs, rather than structurally equivalent. As a result, the distinct submodels fail to convey sufficient insight into the underlying decision-making process of the original deep neural network model. In contrast, the proposed method, referred to as 'correlation-driven feature exchange,' consists of three key components: correlation analysis, feature alignment, and feature refinement. In accordance with these guidelines, the proposed MIMO model learns feature exchanges that not only surpass the existing state-of-the-art in correlation terms, but also demonstrate improved stability and can be successfully applied in visual feature extraction as well. Furthermore, the proposed method facilitates the development of the first-ever end-to-end explainable AI systems for image classification tasks across four distinct datasets, with the code and method being freely accessible at https://github.comjingguo21/CFE.

Over the last decade, significant progress has been made in developing digital repositories for historical manuscript collections, which have paved the way for extensive academic research in the field. By providing a central access point for scholars to study individual manuscripts, these collections also facilitate comparative research on a broader, more global scale. This preliminary study offers an in-depth analysis of existing digitized manuscript collections, covering their scope, limitations, and the potential for future advancements in this area.

Due to the inherent flexibility in robotic joints, elastic coupling affects not just dynamic performance but also severely impacts positional accuracy. Current advanced control techniques fail to fully mitigate the impact of flexiblity when dealing with high-performance applications. In this paper, an innovative approach is introduced, focusing on utilizing supplementary sensors to enhance positional precision by incorporating a correction factor into the control loop. This approach utilizes two main elements - the establishment of a reference model based on system rigidity and the design of a flatness-driven controller that ensures system stability and meets the set positional criteria. As demonstrated through a hybrid robot model, this method is highly effective, especially when paired with traditional velocity-based control. This novel approach was successfully tested on a real-world scenario involving an IRB6600 robot.

A novel method has been created to analyze extensive data on individuals' health histories. By utilizing this approach, researchers can better understand how different health issues can contribute to a single major health event, such as a heart attack. This technique enables identification of specific health markers that increase the risk of such an event and identifies at what stage in the progression of these markers the risk is heightened. A key innovation lies in the technique's ability to simultaneously examine multiple factors contributing to the health event. Using real-world data on myocardial infarction patients, the technique demonstrated that an individual's first experience with ischemic stroke or heart disease significantly increases their chance of suffering a heart attack, with the risk increasing with each subsequent occurrence of these factors.

Molecular dynamics simulations relying on Newton's equations require precise non-conservative force calculations to model phenomena like chemical reactions, which are often characterized by a combination of high and low frequency oscillations. In order to improve efficiency, multi-time-step techniques can separate the forces into slower and faster components, but due to the distinct properties of each, it's difficult to find a single acceptable method to approximate both types of forces without impacting the simulation's accuracy. In the spirit of the multiple-clustering ideas underlying Prendergast's 1967 method, we present a novel approach that categorizes atoms into groups based on their reciprocal bonding frequencies to ensure accurate modeling of both slow and fast dynamics within a single time-step schedule. By implementing this method on clusters from the 2006 CW06 force field, which includes 20-50 atoms, we've found it to be as effective as the CW06 method, yet exhibits improved stability and significantly reduced computational complexity. Moreover, we've demonstrated that the simulation accurately replicates the molecular continuum by successfully generating stable water structures that closely match real-world observations, while also validating our results with experiments and independent force calculations. Overall, this method allows for a major reduction in the computational requirements needed to model systems containing a wide range of frequencies, effectively bringing the modeling of all atomic oscillations within reach even on slower computers.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from both. The problem of finding the minimum resolving set size is known as the metric dimension problem, which can be parameterized to solve it more efficiently. Researchers have investigated parameters like the number of vertices and feedback arcs in a graph to tackle this problem. A new study employs the feedback vertex set parameter, which assesses a graph's worst-case behavior when removing vertices to eliminate all feedback arcs. The researchers show that parameterizing the problem by the size of the feedback vertex set and other attributes yields pseudo-polynomial time complexity. Specifically, the problem can be solved in time proportional to $2^{O(k)} n^{2}$, where $k$ is the feedback vertex set size, $n$ is the vertex count, and assuming a fixed arithmetic operation takes time proportional to the number of its inputs. Similarly, the problem can be parameterized by the graph's tree width, giving time proportional to $2^{O(q)} n^{2}$, with $q$ being the tree width. The researchers established that the problem cannot be solved independently in time proportional to the feedback vertex set size and vertex count under certain conditions but can be solved independently when the graph's clique number, treewidth, and number of vertices are considered. The problem can be solved independently when the graph's clique number, treewidth, and number of vertices are considered. A

A new model for directed surfaces is introduced as a generalization of earlier work on directed areas, enabling the integration of infinitesimal elements with both orientation and direction.  Representing directed surfaces as vector fields in three-dimensional space reveals they have no "up" and "down" distinction like their planar counterparts.  By categorizing regular elements into three types - rotation-free, planar-like, and semi-rotation-free - a directed surface's power is quantified, reflecting its alignment at regular points.  An explicit formula for power is derived for surfaces with constant normal curvature, and a directed surface's power is shown to be bounded above by its total curvature.  Like power, a new concept, direction, measures a surface's deviation from being rotation-free, using an integral formula similar to those for curvature and power.  A surface's direction is also demonstrated to be bounded above its total curvature.  Simple examples illustrate the applications of these new definitions.

To enhance our understanding of heavy rainfall patterns predicted to rise in a hotter climate, our study analyzed the underlying dynamics of deep atmospheric circulation models. The results revealed that in tropical regions, deep convection tends to weaken as temperatures increase, leading to a lower threshold for moistening and the emergence of intense rain showers. These rain showers have a wider range of droplet sizes, resulting in the prediction that heavy downpours will significantly more often make up a large proportion of total precipitation. Our findings also suggested that a higher energy intake in a hotter climate leads to an overall increase in the average size of rain shower areas and total precipitation amounts, causing a surge in the extremity of precipitation patterns.

We have shown that certain high-spin generalizations of self-dual Yang-Mills and its self-dual superpartner in three-dimensional and four-dimensional spacetimes can be represented as twistor operators. Additionally, these results lead to a solution to a functional equation that describes Yang-Mills equations in complex three-dimensional space.

In medical image classification, the presence of label noise can cause imbalanced and non-IID datasets, resulting in deep neural networks favoring easy samples. The typical approach to addressing this issue involves synthetic data augmentation, but this method is limited when dealing with rare medical conditions due to their inherent scarcity. An alternative method using hard-label distribution correction has its drawbacks, including the need to predict hard labels from a soft distribution. To address these problems, we propose a new framework called BLRM that incorporates a Bayesian network to mitigate label noise through a restored version of the true label. The performance of BLRM is compared against current state-of-the-art methods on various benchmark datasets, with the results indicating significant improvements when tested on datasets containing noise. When evaluated against an enhanced synthetic augmentation strategy, BLRM demonstrates superior performance on rare medical image categorization tasks.

Consider a function f, defined as piecewise-smooth with smooth components s_i and a variable n, varying over natural numbers. Let X be an n-dimensional vector space. We define specific sets $I_{\alpha}^{n}$ and $\tilde{I_{\alpha}}^{n}$, involving functions on the unit sphere S^{n-1}, with alpha equal to (n-1)(n+1)/2. For each partial derivative of order k in m dimensions, we denote as D^kf the vector with components the k'th order derivatives of f's components. We establish a certain estimate for the norm of a specific interpolation operator in the space of smooth functions. Specifically, for each point x in S^{n-1}, we define a continuous linear operator T_n: V_n → C(S^m) such that for f as mentioned before and x in S^{n-1}, we have T_n(x) equal to the interpolation of D^kf for k from 0 to n with base points varying with n and f. We show that the norm of T_n for each f with smooth components s_i and a variable n, varying over natural numbers and a fixed m, is bounded.

A random walk transitioning between connected graph nodes exhibits pairwise interactions. The probability of a transition from node i to node j, denoted p_ij, is similar to a matrix element p(I,j) of a polynomial-based transformation of the generating function for a related walk on a graph. This transition probability p_ij is a coefficient in the expansion of the generating function's featured polynomial. Its connection leads to a recursive relationship, allowing the calculation of a symmetric matrix M. In the case of a non-relativistic particle with mass m, the elements of the matrix M represent the potential energies between graph nodes. This relationship extends to a scalar field theory.

In this research paper, we introduce a high-level functional programming language based on LCF's type theory and specifically within the HOL logic system, to efficiently process mathematical definitions with both temporal and logical dependencies, thereby expanding the conventional definition syntax of HOL to accommodate timing information. The language's timer functionality is also examined, along with various strategies for incorporating timers into definitions. A considerable number of practical examples are presented to validate the effectiveness of this approach, encompassing basic concepts, geometric ideals, polynomial-gosper matrices and iterative algorithms. Furthermore, we explore the potential drawbacks of this methodology, highlighting the difficulties and limitations of working with timers, especially in context of equality definitions and functions with redundant parameters, as well as the problem of redundant computation. Ultimately, the results of this investigation provide valuable insights for future TimHOL developments and systematize a range of previously unexplored techniques.

A novel iteration of the coherent boundary layer model has been developed by integrating a statistical technique designed to optimize model predictions. Incorporating the instantaneous effects of turbulent fluctuations at the boundary layer's edge, the iteration takes into account the impact of these fluctuations, assigning higher values to turbulent thermal capacity than would be predicted through conventional means. By combining the modified model with a statistical analysis of data collected from turbulent boundary layer experiments, the model has been refined to simulate various stages of turbulent instability within flat plate experiments. Specifically, the model has been calibrated to simulate four distinct levels of turbulent instability: laminar, transitional, clearly transitional, and fully turbulent, allowing for precise predictions at each stage. These findings have been published in a recent study, providing an update to previous work first presented at the 2018 Symposium on Advances for Predicting Fluid Dynamics

We've modified the Born-Infeld infant Skyrme model by incorporating a topological term and a self-dual equation has been proposed for its non-abelian version. The solitons resulting from this model exhibit Skyrme property but not the full non-abelian one due to the presence of the Born-Infeld infant constraint. Although the constraint yields the correct energy and topological charge for the solitons, it leads to a potentially infinite energy at the boundary according to the originally proposed coupling. However, this issue is resolved by imposing a refined boundary constraint, resulting in a finite energy for the solitons. Alternatively, we've demonstrated that the finite energy can be achieved without the boundary constraint by using a cut-off regulation in the SU(2) gauge theory. This discovery highlights the potential for the infant version of the model to describe stable, topological Skyrme solitons despite its inconsistencies.

Research on Dirac semimetalry has been well-documented in literature, with notable discussions about the semimetal's behavior under a strong magnetic field. In this context, studying the semimetal in high magnetic fields is essential to understand metal-insulator, semimetal-semimetal phase transitions. The presence of edge states in half Dirac semimetalry, which is not forbidden by time-reversal symmetry, has been observed. The behavior of Weyl semimetalry in a strong magnetic field, on the other hand, is more complex and involves (2k$_{F}$+m)$\times$(2k$_{S}$+m) superlattices. Recent analysis suggests that, under a strong magnetic field, one of the two cones may exhibit Kerritz-type phase states transition. The phase transition is caused by Kerritz-sky type mechanism which breaks time-reversal symmetry, potentially indicating that the Kerritz type mechanism can be extended to other topological phase transitions. The mechanism leading to the Kerritz type phase states transition does not only explain the Kerritz type phase states transition in strong magnetic field, but also implies that Kerritz type phase states transition can be induced without a strong magnetic field.

We developed and investigated novel luminous nanostructures based on a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic antenna, consisting of a straight rod with a metal tip. By employing rigorous computational methods, the optical properties of these antennas were examined under different material combinations, including gold-silicon and silicon-gold configurations. The results showed that silicon-gold antennas exhibit enhanced luminosity and illumination level polarization dependence, thus making them suitable for optical imaging and coherent imaging applications, due to their unidirectional light emission. Additionally, the influence of chemical synthesis and material arrangement on these antennas was investigated, and it was found that a 50 nm silicon cap is sufficient to achieve the best performance. Furthermore, the silicon-gold antenna was compared to a conventional aperture lens, and it was discovered that silicon-gold antennas can produce brighter and more coherent light, with a higher polarization anisotropy at telecommunication wavelengths. Finally, the potential of these antennas in coherent imaging and lasing applications was discussed.

To deepen our understanding of Euler's collision invariance as applied to granular materials, we have conducted a study investigating how forces are transmitted during collisions within a layer of granular particles.  By validating a 2D model with a real-time experiment, we have verified a theory proposing that collisions between compacted granular particles exhibit anomalous shielding, where a component of force transmission depends on total impact velocity.  Moreover, we have used computational methods to find that this effect is due to a widespread, localized, dynamic geometric invariant in granular materials, characterized by temporary particle groups forming during collisions.  By incorporating this concept into a numerical simulation, we have demonstrated that accounting for this phenomenon can enhance accuracy in simulating granular collisions.

Systematic calculations were conducted to examine the electronic properties of manganese-doped silicene deposited on a boron nitride surface. The results show that the presence of manganese adorments alters the band gap structure of silicene in a Deposition-Induced Gapless Phase, and introduces new gap-opened bands in the two-dimensional structure. Additionally, the computational findings demonstrate that silicene with manganese adorments can exhibit ferromagnetic ordering due to strong interactions between manganese and neighboring silicon atoms.

The explosion of a red supergiant star resulting in a core collapse not only releases radiation, but also generates massive particle acceleration within the expanding shell. Recent observations of the $^{26}$Al transient event in the northern hemisphere, linked to the explosion of a red supergiant in the galaxy, have been closely tracked over the past 50 years. Our study aims to identify the source of this explosion, one that matches the described characteristics of a redder and more luminous supergiant than our sun, by analyzing data from various sources such as infrared images, $^{26}$Al emission maps, historical star explosion records, and high-resolution molecular gas maps. Our analysis points towards Sgr A East, a partially visible supernova remnant in the center of the Milky way, as the most likely source of the explosion. Although the exact timing of the explosion is still unclear, it is believed to have occurred approximately 100-200 years ago. Our study confirms that massive stars do not remain in the galaxy, as they either explode as supernovae or merge with the central black hole.

The imbalance between data categories hinders accurate text classification, and solving this problem is known as the "class imbalance issue."  The class imbalance problem is a widespread issue in machine learning that must be addressed.  The class imbalance problem occurs when one class has more instances than the others, causing the model to favor the majority class.  The class imbalance issue is prevalent in real-world datasets, especially in text classification.  The over-sampling method is commonly used to mitigate the class imbalance problem.  The objective of this research is to examine various over-sampling techniques for accurate text classification.  The paper presents a detailed examination of nine over-sampling methods that enhance instance generation for improved multi-category text classification.  The evaluation of these methods involved comparing their performance using different metrics, including accuracy, the F1 score, the area under the ROC curve, and the Kullback-Leibler divergence.  The dataset comprised 1,553 instances of three categories, divided into distinct sub-sets to test the impact of each method's density on classification performance.

This study analyzes how regional news outlets covered the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States from January 2020 to August 2020, and its findings to date have been presented in part. We examine the correlation between COVID-19 coverage, regional outcomes, and audience behavior in the United States, also taking into account the distinct characteristics of different news outlets and regions. Notably, this research discovers a substantial variation in COVID-19 reporting across 196 U.S. regions, associated with multiple factors such as demographic differences, infection rates, and pre-existing conditions. Furthermore, it reveals a significant connection between regional news coverage of COVID-19 and subsequent infection increases and fatalities, and an inverse relationship with subsequent changes in audience size for non-governmental regional news outlets, and an opposite trend for governmental regional news outlets. These results have substantial implications, suggesting that regional news coverage of COVID-19 may have influenced audiences' perceptions and behaviors regarding the virus.

The Rapid Multipole Method, a version of the Fast Multipole Method (FMM), has been widely used due to its simplicity and clarity in teaching and implementation, especially with the recent updates ensuring its accuracy. Although the original algorithm preserved linear momentum exactly, the conservation of angular momentum was not guaranteed. A correction was applied in 2014 to ensure the linear momentum is conserved, but the conservation of angular momentum remained a topic until it was resolved for collisions in 2015, and a general proof for non-colliding cases has been presented the same year. A correction was applied in 2017 to the quadratic term of the angular momentum, and a proof of conservation for the updated algorithm followed in 2018. However, the conservation proof required the use of a potentially inaccurate approximation of coupling terms, and an improvement to the method's accuracy led to a revision of the proof in 2020, despite no change to the algorithm itself.

In electron-proton scattering, it's been demonstrated that 100% of longitudinal polarization is transferred from the initial polarized proton to the final proton, provided certain conditions are met - namely, that the square of the four-momentum transfer must exceed 0.1 GeV$^2$.

To achieve substantial gains with small datasets, combining multiple models can be beneficial. Specifically, in the context of medical image analysis, a primary challenge is integrating different deep learning models in a harmonious way. Typically, a base model, or "generalist," provides a balance of capabilities and is trained extensively to strike a medium course. On the other hand, "specialist" models are trained exclusively to perfect a specific task, such as enhancing details, reducing noise, or tackling complex data with contrasting characteristics. However, the process of training a specialist model to complement a base model's capabilities is complicated, involving the adjustment of various hyperparameters. In our research, we demonstrate that a straightforward approach to data augmentation can greatly optimize the performance of a base model by regulating the impact of a specialist's training on image quality. Moreover, in an effort to reduce the financial burden of acquiring large medical images, we introduce a novel, record-based approach to data augmentation, which allows for more flexible creation of training datasets. Our experiments, conducted on two critical applications in medical fields, show that our approach yields superior results, with higher overall detection rates and more precise boundaries without compromising aspect ratio ratios.

Measurements of cross-sections for processes producing a Higgs boson pair together with a vector boson (W or Z) or a vector boson (W or Z) and a photon have been conducted using the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. The analyzed data, corresponding to 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions recorded at 13 TeV, are in agreement with the predictions of the Standard Model and allow for assessments of the Higgs boson pair production cross-section as 0.64 pb, along with the related cross-section ratios.

Atomic masers based on rotational transitions in molecules like hydrogen cyanide and ammonia offer advanced scientific tools, digital precision timekeeping, and quantum information applications. A digital alkaline spin maser has been developed using the $F$-sublevel $J=1\rightarrow0$ transition in laser-cooled $^{39}$Ca$^+$ ions at 674 THz. The new system incorporates a highly stable microwave clock driven by an ultra-low-noise electric field generated by a $LC$-resonator. The maser's performance was evaluated by two methods - by modulating the noise with amplitude fluctuations and by using it to regulate a feedback loop reducing the noise. When evaluated in both ways, the team discovered that the system could achieve thermal equilibrium at temperatures below 1 microkelvin. The alkaline maser has the potential to contribute to precision spectroscopy, could be scaled up for secure quantum communication, and also serves as a sophisticated tool for studying atomic physics.

We present an algorithm that determines the number of special elements in the group of rational points of the symmetric space $SL_{n}(\mathbb{R})}/(/V_{n}/\mathbb{Z})$, where $V_{n}$ represents the Weyl chamber associated with a specific, chosen root system of simple dimensions. Subsequently, our algorithm enables us to calculate the count of elements in the group of rational points of the quotient $K3^{sm}/\mathbb{Z}$ for any given projective K3 variety $K3^{sm}$ that arises from embedding a K3 surface $K3$ into a projective space, provided that variety $K3^{sm}$ has a Picard number of $18$. Furthermore, our algorithm facilitates the computation of the degree of the associated Siegel discriminant form for all such K3 varieties once they are identified.

By incorporating a gauge singlet scalar field with a false vacuum as a pseudoscalar inflaton, we investigate an intriguing neutralino dark matter arrangement that also addresses the accelerating universe's current state. The neutralino's mass is ephemeral, deteriorates over time, yet its mass remains less than the pseudoscalar inflaton's mass. The neutralino's mass is generated via a substantial $A$-term as a result of an enormous VEV of a hidden gauge theory's $U(1)$. The neutralino's mass, once created, is gradually reduced by a detuning process linked to the pseudoscalar inflaton's motion within the concept of the Shift-Symmetry. The pseudoscalar inflaton's motion causes the deterioration rate, thereby rendering the neutralino's mass transient. The neutralino's mass is ultimately extinguished when its mass is surpassed by the pseudoscalar inflaton's mass, marking the termination of its deterioration. The neutralino's mass and deterioration rate are heavily influenced by an enormous $U(1)$-hidden gauge theory's coupling constant. The neutralino and pseudoscalar inflaton are accompanied by numerous unstable particles originating from the hidden $U(1)$ gauge theory, leading to the production of dark matter and ultimately result in the emission of gamma rays, which are observable. The investigation of the neutralino's gamma radiation spectrum provides insights into its inherent properties, namely, mass and deterioration rate. A study of future space-based gamma observatories could potentially verify these parameters

A compact surface is called a thick graph if it can be obtained by simplifying a particular type of surface, known as a surface with a homeomorphism to a graph, through a process called normal surface compression. Despite the proof of a polynomial-time upper bound for the genus of such surfaces, a similar upper bound has remained unsolved for thick graphs until now. This paper presents an algorithm that efficiently estimates the genus of a thick graph by designing polynomial-time approximate and adaptive measurements. This method first applies a constant-factor approximation, then gradually refines the guess for the genus until it accurately determines the genus. As an alternative, we developed another algorithm that efficiently finds an integer estimate for the genus of a thick graph. This method works by utilizing a particular type of graph called saddle graphs, which are derived from the surface compression of a given surface. By showing that a particular class of these graphs has a polynomial-time upper bound for their genus, we created a new algorithm. This algorithm works by approximating a particular function at every vertex of a graph to obtain an integer estimate for the genus of a thick graph, proving the genus upper bounded by a particular number that only depends on another particular number. This method can be applied to obtain efficient estimates for particular graph problems, demonstrating its utility.

This note presents a decentralized algorithm for solving large, solvable convex optimization problems across multiple agents with distinct processing capabilities. The proposed Newton's method variant is characterized by complex, distinct computations for each agent, while only requiring them to share gradient information. Consequently, the algorithm's convergence rate remains bounded by $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ as $t\to\infty$, which is the optimal rate for decentralized settings over multiple rounds. Notably, the method's stability is ensured through the incorporation of random perturbations in the communication step, thus ensuring its convergence in the presence of arbitrary delays in data transmission. We verify the method's performance through a comprehensive set of distributed convex optimization examples, including a detailed analysis of a 1-ball projection example relevant to various applications.

Our research focuses on developing a novel hate-speech detection technique using
neural networks that utilizes sequential data from text, which we successfully
applied to datasets in both Hindi and Bengali. The performance of our model is
comparable to current state-of-the-art techniques on the Hindi dataset and shows
promising results on the Bengali dataset, opening up new possibilities for
research. The study also reveals that our model outperforms similar methods using
word embeddings constructed from the entire Wikipedia in both languages, and we
explore the effect of using transfer learning with a multilingual BERT model
subsequently fine-tuned on the respective Hindi and Bengali datasets.

In particle detector technology that is both highly precise and extremely large, 
operating the gas time projection chambers in ultralow density with long paths 
is a key strategy to fully record particle interactions in 3D space. However, a major 
obstacle arises due to particle recoil during interactions with electrons, causing a 
significant loss of detection information. In order to overcome this, the selection 
of a suitable release mechanism for ionization, a crucial factor in the design of TPCs 
is crucial. In this study, different measurable indicators related to the transfer 
of momentum due to particle recoil are examined, with the goal of distinguishing 
between the main ionizable components of matter - helium, carbon, nitrogen, and 
oxygen - based on their mass ratios. These indicators are: the standard measure of 
recoil kinetic energy, the average velocity, the root mean square velocity, the 
most probable velocity, the scattering cross-section, and the velocity distribution 
width. Furthermore, the advantages and disadvantages of each measurable are 
examined, with a suggested approach for selecting and designing the release 
mechanisms in future TPCs that utilize ultralow density and long paths.

The widespread adoption of commercial driving by technology is crucial for commercial success, yet the integration of this technology with human judgment remains a challenging issue. To improve the quality of commercial services, a contextual evaluation framework is developed, focusing on the equilibrium achieved through the combination of machine outputs and human input. By incorporating this framework, the equilibrium is analyzed based on the impact it has on society, using a two-player game theory model as a reference. A pilot study was conducted to test the framework's effectiveness, involving the analysis of images from a traffic monitoring system to assess the accuracy of commercial driving services. To determine the best approach, the accuracy of machine outputs and human-machine collaboration were compared, ultimately revealing that collaborative assessment surpasses individual assessment in terms of accuracy. Consequently, the proposed framework serves as a solution to the integration problem of commercial driving services and human judgment, demonstrating its practical utility through the pilot study's results.

We present a collection of findings from the Out-of-Lexicon Romanization Challenge, which took place during the 2020 Conference on Machine Learning, Algorithms, and Systems for Information Processing. The competition involved tasks requiring to correct historical names found in textual sources, drawing from birth, marriage, and death records, as well as literary works, across three languages: German, Italian, and Spanish. The demonstration includes a comprehensive comparison of the performance achieved by the winning entry and the overall outcome of the competition, utilizing the transformative testing technique proposed by Koch (2020). Additionally, we show how the newly developed testing strategy can be applied to the systems themselves to assess their resilience, providing insight into the characteristics of each approach that contribute to their performance.

Understanding complex systems benefits from statistical modeling, often involving a Gaussian field that can be mapped to a manifold, facilitating geometric statistics and optimization approaches. Although geometric metrics can be chosen freely, the widely used Euclidean metric may not suit every case, as it doesn't account for the underlying field's covariance. In contrast, the approach presented here involves leveraging Riemannian geometric tools to analyze Gaussian field dynamics using the natural metric. This can be achieved by interpreting the natural metric in a stochastic variational setting. By choosing a specific Lagrangian, the method can accommodate various factorizations, including Euclidean and Gaussian probability distributions. As a result, the geodesics defined by this framework have appealing inductive biases, mirroring the forward dynamics in a generative model or the regularizing effects of Tikhonov regularization when considering a well-posed problem. Theoretical foundations of this approach are explored, including sufficient conditions for optimizing a Lagrangian, and the phenomenon of metric oscillation is discussed. Empirical demonstrations of this method's efficacy can be found in a Gaussian process regression context.

When applying a nonlocal excitation operator to an initial state, the response is correctly captured by a damped oscillation for a short observation period, but the system behaves erratically and fails to accurately replicate the initial conditions for a longer observation time. A modified version of the nonlocal operator, combined with Fourier expansion, successfully produces accurate results in all time frames. However, in some instances, the original operator produces a more accurate outcome sooner. For the purpose of this study, the original operator is referred to as 'improving towards reality,' whereas the modified operator is termed'short-time accuracy toward reality.' In contrast, the term 'gaining accuracy toward reality' will be applied to the original operator in this context. A thorough examination was conducted to explore a potential connection between a material's physical properties and the operator's performance. This investigation analyzed and contrasted the impact of various parameters, including the observer's velocity relative to the material, the observer's position relative to the material, electric polarizability, electric conductivity, and nonlocality in electric processes. Ultimately, this research aims to understand how an evaluation method's duration influences its reliability and to identify any correlations between a material's properties and the results of nonlocal response models. To achieve this goal, the study implements a realistic approach to nonlocal response evaluation using specific mathematical operators that replicate observed behaviors in experiments and simulations. As an example, this research specifically analyzes and discusses hydrodynamic conductivities of graphene due to the lack of

Using Adel's conjecture and class number formula, we establish a upper limit on the absolute value of factors derived from L-functions associated with Hecke characters of certain complex numbers, and we also prove a similar result for L-functions associated with weight two cusp forms.

We investigated spin-dependent transport in AGNs, focusing on their ability to conduct spin-based operations at a relatively high density. By analyzing a two-terminal configuration with a coupled double quantum dot system as the central component, we found that energy spacing between Dots 1 and 2 can enable multiple transmission peaks, allowing for the broadest span of magnetic field applications compared to other designs. Moreover, applying a regulatory gate can shift the magnetic field application range for the spin-down channel by altering the energy level of Dot 2. What's more, we discovered that in certain conditions, the system can exhibit noticable within-band magnetoconductance, meaning even when the system's energy spacing isn't adjustable, a regulatory gate can still be used to apply magnetic field operations. This research demonstrates the potential for using AGNs to perform spin-based operations at high density.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues for nonlinear, monotonic operators that map $n$-dimensional space or the $n$-dimensional unit cube to itself. The discussion includes a theorem specific to the case of bivariate functions and offers a meaningful extension to the category of continuous functions. The findings presented herein are original and represent a significant advancement in the theory of approximation theory.

Let $G$ be a graph with a vertex activity of $\alpha$. The problem discusses the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle in a graph $G$, and its relationship with the concept of pancyclic properties. A useful quantity called the independence number of a graph $G$, denoted as $\alpha(G)$, is introduced. A key result establishes a lower bound on the activity of a graph $G$ in terms of its size and the diameter. Specifically, it has been proven that if the size of graph $G$ is $n$ and the diameter is $\gamma$, then the activity of $G$ satisfies $\alpha(G) \ge \frac{n \log \gamma}{6} + \sqrt{2n \log \gamma}$. This result yields useful information about the properties of cyclic graphs.

This research examines optical (anti-)protons produced in collisions of gold nuclei at 200 GeV using a specific optical model.  The study reveals a notable tendency of anti-protons to be released closer to the collision point than protons and shows this effect aligns with the properties of optical hadrons produced in similar interactions, also explaining observed protons produced in isobar collisions.  The study further notes that optical hadrons retain minimal memory of the details of the collision process, suggesting their formation occurs rapidly.  The study concludes that optical (anti-)protons originate from the interaction of a specific type of quark and antiquark, denoted as soft $q \bar{q}$ pairs, lasting a short period of time.  The conditions necessary for the formation of these $q \bar{q}$ pairs are derived from the properties of the two massive nuclei and their speed of approach, explaining the observed characteristics.  The study also notes a specific relationship between the production rates of optical protons and the energy released in non-elastic interactions that generally adheres to generally accepted rules but exhibits some exceptions likely due to the production of strange nuclei.  The study concludes by noting that optical (anti-)protons offer a specific test of conditions within heavy nuclei and can be studied in greater detail at the updated RHIC facility.

The adaptive spectral Koopman technique offers a novel approach for dynamic system analysis and control design by leveraging complex data from diverse sources. It's particularly useful for handling non-linear systems, even in cases where only partial information is available. One of its key benefits is the ability to perform in-depth state-of-charge estimations and control low-dimensional systems of high dimensionality. Although it's well-suited for a wide range of applications, the spectral Koopman method has some limitations when it comes to computing requirements, especially in large-scale contexts. To overcome this, we've developed a new approach that combines the adaptive spectral Koopman technique with sparse grid finite volumes for more efficient state estimation and control in high-dimensional systems. Our proposed methodology has been successfully tested on two examples: a system with multiple switched parameters and a general battery model. The results demonstrate the significant potential of sparse grid-based Koopman methods for real-time control and estimation in complex dynamic systems.

A new strategy, the outside complicated scaling method, has been developed to accommodate strong DC fields when dealing with atoms and molecules through a non-perturbative approach. This rigorous approach is essentially a refinement of the outside inverse Inverse Hyperbolic Mapping, providing a more practical solution by shifting singularities away from the Schrödinger equation's pole. This new strategy has been successfully applied to several systems, including the Rydberg atom in a strong DC field, the helium ion, and the hydrogen molecule in extremely high voltage fields.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is widely used to solve the Schrödinger problem, which established the unavailability of closed-form solutions for a broader class of OT problems. In the present study, we demonstrate that this algorithm converges not only to a stationary point of the modified Sinkhorn problem but also, under specific conditions, to a K-matrix. Nevertheless, a recent study (Chizat et al., 2018) presented alternative paths for the algorithm's convergence, which do not necessitate the explicit calculation of the modified Sinkhorn problem's numerical solution. Our work addresses a long-standing question regarding the algorithm's behavior when no closed-form solution exists for the Schrödinger problem, which was previously assumed to underlie all OT problems.

Measurements of top-quark pair production cross-sections are carried out as part of a 2011 pp collision study at a 5.02 TeV center-of-mass energy using the ATLAS detector. A data sample of 7.7 fb^-1 was used for this purpose, including both charged particles and photons in an analysis to increase statistical significance. Calculated cross-sections based on top-quark pair events reveal an observed value of 43.4 ± 1.8(stat) ± 1.3(syst) ± 1.3(bin) pb, being relatively consistent with theoretical predictions from QCD. Additionally, an estimated integrated cross-section of 43.4 ± 3.0 (stat) ± 2.1 (syst) ± 1.1 (bin) pb was generated using lepton+jets events, totalizing 25.2 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity.

This study is set in a complex environment with multiple components and
interconnected flux lines connected to a central active node. Using a
logarithmic transformation, we convert the resulting SLF equation to a solvable
MKF equation, and then derive specific critical conditions for distinct
phenomena: single localization, multiple simultaneous localizations, and
the occurrence of an endless loop of two.

The janowski maps are a subset of rational mappings with a periodic nature, and a previously established study linked them to generalized Bessel functions through hyperbolic volume computations for Schottky groups. This study extends that work, incorporating said functions into the classification of janowski maps.

To understand how income inequalities affect urban mobility, we analyzed the patterns of patient visits at two major public healthcare systems in Beijing, by gathering data on bus routes and patient distribution across different districts.  Our findings show that richer areas had more patient visits per doctor, as well as greater use of public transport for commuting to such facilities.  Furthermore, patient visits in richer areas received more financial support compared to those in poorer areas.  The COVID pandemic highlighted how income inequalities can impact urban mobility, especially by revealing significant disparities in public health resources across different districts.  By combining spatial analysis tools like bus routes and population density distribution, along with socioeconomic data, urban policymakers can make more informed decisions about urban development and resource allocation to mitigate such inequalities.

This study evaluates the effectiveness of a pioneering field-separated preconditioning technique in managing two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media. The technique is combined with either a RAS-Smith model or with strategic field selection, and is examined alongside more conventional approaches such as comprehensive linear two-phase flow preconditioning and element-based preconditioning using field-specific techniques. Extensive simulations of two-phase flow in uneven media are conducted to thoroughly test the preconditioning methods. The findings indicate that the field-separated preconditioning technique offers significant performance enhancements when compared with conventional methods, and also tend to outperform the RAS-Smith model and strategic field selection approaches.

We've proposed and tested a concept for an optical device known as a unilateral chiral optical chamber. This innovative device has the capacity to efficiently convert circularly polarized light into an orbital angular momentum-rich beam of scattered photons. Our research shows that optical interactions with a unidirectionally scattering medium produce a unique balance of geometric and topological attributes. A demonstration of this topological effect was achieved by constructing an optical chamber with a sparse, randomly arranged scattering surface. Our findings indicate that the chiral properties of the optical chamber can be identified from the two-dimensional scattering pattern of photons, despite the lack of linear polarization-dependent variations. Notably, the chiral characteristics of the optical chamber can also be confirmed through the fractal pattern of photons scattered in specific directions. Our model predicts that the chiral properties of the optical chamber should remain consistent, even when the scattering surface is minimally deformed. These findings could pave the way for the creation of various classical and quantum-based systems that leverage the unique topological properties of light.

We re-examine the relationship between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on flat spacetime and the universal conformal field theory of string theory, incorporating both the first and third decades of the Liouville theory's modular parameter. By mapping Liouville variables to suitably defined differential forms on the Teichmuller space of the disc, we visualize the three regions as distinct phases of a complex matrix model. Notably, the boundary between the first and third phases corresponds with the quantum self-dual point of the matrix model proposed by Brezin, Douglas, and Ooguri.

A solution known as the Robson-Kerr warp bubble is derived from an advanced mathematical approach incorporating a modified version of Einstein's general relativity equations. In this research, we include a specific type of energy field in these equations, which has a constant value and can be either positive or negative. As a result, the shape of the warp bubble in this scenario can either be a sphere, or more complex forms like a lemon or Swiss cheese. A significant aspect of this type of space-time is that it remains stable in the absence of specific types of disturbance, which are known as Hamiltonian perturbations. In this study, we have also identified which types of energy density mark the boundary between stable and unstable systems. A key aspect of this type of space-time is that it can be divided into two distinct regions: one where the gravitational force is weak due to its low density, and another where the gravitational force is strong due to its high density. Additionally, we have shown that the shape of the warp bubble in this scenario can be influenced by the variation of energy density along the axis. In order to verify our results numerically, we have used a mathematical approach known as the method of conformal field equations, or the 1+3 splitting method.

As the world's infrastructure grows in complexity, managing it as a living thing is no longer feasible. To bridge this gap, a new approach called GUIDES (Geospatial Metropolitan Infrastructure Data Engineering Resolutions) has been developed to provide a framework for creating a platform that integrates and visualizes the connections between underground infrastructure systems. This will enable a more comprehensive and pragmatic understanding of the commonalities and differences between various metro areas. The GUIDES platform's initial application in Detroit, Michigan, has demonstrated its potential for queryability and data analysis by identifying patterns and relationships. This has paved the way for creating a common platform that cities can use to model and visualize their infrastructure systems, fostering a greater and more informed understanding of the subterranean environment.

To analyze the motion of an ion lattice, researchers studied how spin decay impacts the coherence of neighboring ions. By varying the laser intensity used to repulse the ions, the team explored a wide range of motion states, from highly excited to frozen. Utilizing both theoretical and experimental approaches, the study examined the impact of individual ion decay on a collective system. Most notably, the results revealed that when the motion of the ion lattice is highly excited, its coherence is primarily influenced by the motion of a single ion and the resulting spin decay. However, when the motion is frozen due to intense repumping, the coherence is mainly affected by the decay of a pair of ions and the resulting loss of correlation. This analysis allowed the team to develop a way to accurately determine the temperature of the ion lattice, as well as the rate at which the lattice is heated due to external influences.

A novel approach has been developed to study the interactions within a tunneling electron microscope (TEM) by utilizing quantum mechanics in conjunction with two closely related models: chemical and electromagnetic interactions. The primary goal is to find precise energy corrections that could potentially rival experimental accuracy. The method starts by inputting electron wave functions derived from two related models - one chemical and one electromagnetic - into an equation. The output, along with other relevant terms, is then used to calculate a relevant quantity that governs the interaction between the electron and molecules. The energy corrections obtained through this method demonstrate a notable correlation with experimental results from local infrared spectroscopy, suggesting their validity. The method employs quantum mechanical principles to generate spatially dependent potential maps that are contingent on the electron's wave function. The energy corrections in local experiments reveal a distinct optimization pattern - they significantly rise at small distances, peak at an intermediate value, and significantly decrease at larger distances. The method is currently limited by its processing intensity due to the necessity of repeating the simulation multiple times for different electron positions, making it suitable for visualizing the potential around a single molecule but more feasible for smaller molecules. The method's code is publicly available, and our study is the first to evaluate the full quantum mechanical interaction in local experiments. The code can be freely accessed at https://github.com/qdqd79/TERS_qm_code.

Our research aims to identify unusual radio signals in nearby galaxies, including spiral and irregular galaxies, using the Sardinia Radio Dish. A frequency scan between 12 and 18 GHz reveals that the galaxy NGC 404 stands out with an unexplained flat spectrum at 16 GHz. Further observation within an 8 month period confirms the existence of a persistent, highly variable microwave signal with a broad distribution of frequencies, centered around 16 GHz, equivalent in size to our solar system. The SMD then conducted joint observations with the IRAM-30m telescope in winter 2020, but did not detect any associated cooling flow or broad distribution of frequencies in the galaxy NGC 404.

The entropic costs associated with various solid-state phase transitions can be evaluated using an entropy (R) scale that has historically been difficult to apply.  A recent study found that the entropic costs in ammonium sulfate exhibited an unexpectedly high value of three times the conventional limit. To explain this discrepancy, our research suggests that the energy-related origin of the entropic costs is the overlap of localized energy pulses, resulting in a removal of low-lying harmonic vibrations, an idea supported by computer simulations. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the primary cause of shifting stability in ammonium sulfate's ferroelectric state is the result of competition between localized and delocalized interactions.

In reinforcement learning, organisms learn from the consequences of their actions, utilize forecasting methods to assess the likelihood and accuracy of expected outcomes, and adapt these expectations when discrepancies arise. Prior research found that suboptimal decision-makers have difficulty adjusting their expectations when anticipating a reward or penalty, leading to an overestimation of likely outcomes. This study examines whether midbrain activity in the dopaminergic system, a part of the brain involved in learning, processing, and regulating rewards and predictions, differs between optimal and suboptimal learners, with a focus on reward prediction errors. We analyzed the brain activity of healthy humans as they played two variants of a Monte Carlo sampling game - one where the reward probabilities were uncertain and another where the reward probabilities were hidden. The results showed that activity in the midbrain among optimal learners was greater when their predictions were incorrect, indicating a better capacity to adjust their expectations and learn. In contrast, suboptimal learners did not show this ability to adjust their predictions or learn, with their midbrain activity appearing unresponsive to prediction errors. Notably, suboptimal learners' brain activity in the midbrain was similar to that of optimal learners when their expectations were confirmed, suggesting a better capacity to take risks and adapt to new information. This research implies that the midbrain is crucial for learning to adjust one's expectations and adapt to new information, with its activity reflecting the efficiency of these learning abilities.

A specific type of mathematical structure, important in physics, can be generated from the root system of a particular Lie group using two methods of extension to create a more complex structure. The resulting complex structure has eight octants, each containing a copy of a group that describes the rotation of three-dimensional space, when truncated to a specific subset of this group. The entire group describing three-dimensional space rotations can be replicated eight ways within this complex structure. The extensions allow for various interpretations in physics, including how particles interact with each other. The resulting structure has properties similar to a specific type of mathematical structure found in neurons, which is important in understanding how neurons communicate with each other. The evidence suggests that this complex structure has properties that may not behave logically, which could explain a specific phenomenon where the rules of physics change depending on the experiment.
