We investigate the problem of finding all items in a massive dataset that are closer to a query object than a certain threshold, in cases where each data object and the query object consist of a set of time series each of a fixed length, and where similarity between sequences is measured using the Frechet distance. We present a range search method that checks the Frechet distance and is different from existing methods, which focus on finding a single closest sequence or collecting signals that signify proximity without a predefined distance threshold. Unlike other techniques, which rely on dynamic data structures that require O(n) space and computation, our approach allows for a more static 3-approximation method that is inspired by the Roth and Meyer techniques. We present a new, more efficient method that requires only O(m) space and can compute the distance between two sequences in O(m) time. Furthermore, our approach can be applied to provide narrow Frechet distance limits, meaning that if a sequence is known to be at a distance d from the query, our method can determine if it is also within a smaller distance e from the query, and our last contribution is an analysis of the time and space efficiency of existing methods that provide such narrow limits.

High-precision quantum memory manipulation is crucial for the practical application of quantum information technologies, particularly when dealing with large datasets in quantum simulations and simulations of complex physical processes. However, the limited capacity of quantum memory, resulting in partial erasure of stored patterns, significantly hampers progress in these areas. To overcome this obstacle, we've developed a Scalable Assessment Error Mitigation (SAEM) method that improves the accuracy of quantum memory manipulation by as much as two orders of magnitude. Inspired by the iterative Bayesian restoration algorithm, used in medical imaging, our approach has a clear theoretical foundation and can be efficiently implemented using maximum likelihood optimization techniques. The effectiveness of SAEM is demonstrated through successful high-precision simulations of complex quantum physics scenarios, such as the calculation of the energy spectrum in a quasiparticle model of hydrogen. Notably, the SAEM technique not only significantly enhances the accuracy of quantum memory manipulation but also is adaptable to a wide range of quantum many-body systems.

There's been a shift in robotics research from individual robots to those that work together as a team.  We investigated how three distinct autonomous methodologies could enhance collaboration by having them interact with one another in a unified robotic system. Our experiments revealed that combining these various approaches could lead to a diverse range of complex behaviors, enabling our robot to adapt to changing situations more effectively, particularly those involving communication and multi-step thinking.

For individuals with developmental disabilities, achieving independence in navigating unfamiliar areas can be a challenge, which can be overcome by utilizing innovative accessibility solutions. We have designed a personalized navigation system called HiTMap, built on the principles of topological navigation. This system comprises a topological diagram containing abstract locations, and their connections representing safe routes between them. Unlike conventional geographic information like Google Street View, HiTMap focuses on the geometry of routes rather than physical streets, making it a crucial tool for independent travel. In comparison to existing systems, HiTMap enables individuals to learn and understand unfamiliar areas more effectively by breaking down navigation into simpler components, thereby reducing the overall complexity. We have tested the HiTMap system with users having intellectual disabilities and received positive feedback, and the system's source code can be accessed on the repository located at https://github.com/taiwanncphd/HitMap.

Inter-group codes are described in a circuit model using multivariable functions, resulting in two types: 2-D arrays with a zero-supplementary element and 3-D arrays with an inter-group supplementary element. 

Inter-group codes are designed to simplify circuit expansion, particularly when expanding a binary circuit to a multi-group version, by converting the circuit into a 3-D array with inter-group supplementary elements, then adding zeros to complete the 3-D array, allowing for direct construction.

To develop inter-group supplementary code sets, we built upon previous work by extending single-variable functions to multivariable functions, applying this to arrays with zero-supplementary elements, specifically examining 2-D arrays, to establish a comprehensive understanding, ultimately finding that a 2-D array code set can be used to generate a 3-D array code set.

We demonstrated that a 2-D array code set can be utilized to create three types of 3-D arrays: those with inter-group and zero-supplementary elements through addition, repetition, and permutation, also revealing that three 2-D arrays with different shapes can form a 3-D array with inter-group and zero-supplementary elements.

To develop zero-supplementary array code sets, we identified that zero-supplementary elements can be generated by setting specific variable values in single-variable functions, also establishing that a zero-supplementary array code set can be formed by combining arrays with zero-supplementary elements.

Through the analysis of 2-D arrays with zero-supplementary elements, we

A proposed four-step process aims to address problems of image quality, noise, and material degradation in computed tomography images through the use of multiple energy levels. By incorporating a breakthrough based on the Tamura variance principle, an innovative norm is introduced that captures details across a wide spectrum while minimizing the effects of noise. A low-rank matrix decomposition technique, inspired by NMF, is used in conjunction with an anti-noise noiser to effectively handle noise and reconstruct broken materials in CT scans. A dual problem is created through the use of Fenchel-Dunnal representation, allowing the method to be transformed into an efficient iterative scheme that minimizes the overall error. Experimental data from multiple sources demonstrate that this technique leads to superior outcomes, particularly when applied to images taken with multiple energy levels.

This work investigates the impact of electron movement and non-local properties on a gap-plasmon mode when a charge imbalance between two areas disappears. Employing a perturbative approach and a perturbation theory scheme, we analyze the dependence of the system's dispersion on the size of the two areas and their relative separation. We demonstrate that for tiny distances and non-local electron behavior, the system's frequency spectrum exhibits a logarithmic decline. Furthermore, our findings reveal the emergence of new modes at non-zero electron velocities, and the system's frequency spectrum shows a gradual shift towards higher frequencies in this case.

In this research, we investigate how comments from users influence the learning process of a model that identifies and understands key phrases in text, focusing on names, when the full training data is not available. The model's ability to learn is impacted by the importance it assigns to specific words in its vocabulary. The importance of these words is typically determined automatically and can be inaccurate, leading to suboptimal performance. To overcome this, we reveal that users are capable of identifying crucial words accurately and utilize their feedback to adjust the model's learning process. The model first generates potential names and context based on text, asking users to select the most important parts. The users' selective feedback is then incorporated into the model, enhancing its ability to accurately identify names and context by weighting the significance of specific words in its vocabulary. The model achieves superior performance in comparing the model with user feedback to baseline models that utilize random feedback or no feedback at all.

Interactive visualizations play a crucial role in analyzing complex data by assisting users in gaining insights they may have otherwise overlooked. Among the various data types analyzed, time sequence data stands out for its complexity due to its multidimensional nature. This research aims to explore how users interact with such data in comparison to linear data and proposes a new visualization system, Hierarchical Time ID. To evaluate and understand user interactions, we developed a single-player game called "Clinch, the Time Traveler." We conducted workshops to gather feedback and observed users' behavior in real-world conditions. The findings indicate that incorporating visual cues, facilitating faster data navigation, and offering alternative methods can enhance user experience, particularly when working with multidimensional data. This research offers insights and insights that can inform the creation of interactive visualizations for complex data types.

The value of disease prediction and diagnosis is recognized, but current models have limitations due to their exclusive use of clinical data when making decisions. There's a pressing need for models that also incorporate diverse types of information typically found in digital health records, including medical images, genetic data, and other assets. In response, we've developed a novel method called the Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network (DSGNN), which can seamlessly integrate various forms of structured and unstructured data into a unified representation. In our study, we leveraged the FeDER dataset to compare the performance of our model against existing methods, using medical images from the Radiology of the University of Pennsylvania dataset to predict Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease for patients. By focusing on graph neural networks that capture diverse similarity between digital health records, we've significantly enhanced the accuracy of disease diagnosis and discovery.

Within the framework of Debye-Huckel theory, considering the effects of solvent polarization, our research provides an analytical expression for the electrostatic potential near a charged soft interface in an electrolyte solution. This modified potential display exhibits a distinct dip at the interface when the charge is negative, accompanied by a Hall effect-like pattern in the vicinity of the point zero potential. The inclusion of solvent effects in Debye-Huckel theory enhances the stability of the electric double layer at low ionic concentrations, especially for negative charges.

Automating software specification extraction has been attempted through various methods since the 1970s, with a recent revival of interest. This study assesses a novel neural technique for extracting specifications from a given code's comments and compares it to established methods that leverage natural language processing. Comment datasets used in this comparison include those from the software repository Buggilla and the specification extraction competition SpecEval '21. This work also explores how pre-trained language models can be employed for initial specification extraction before being fine-tuned for improved performance. Additionally, it examines how pre-trained and fine-tuned models can be utilized for automatic specification completion. This study evaluates several metrics, including F1-score, accuracy, and the average Robinson-Fowkes (RF) metric, to quantify the models' performance in terms of correct identification, correct rejection, and false positives. Consequently, the main contributions of this research are as follows. Firstly, it revisits software specification extraction from a natural language perspective, addressing the challenge of data scarcity in software engineering. Secondly, it benchmark several recent pre-trained models on the SpecEval '21 dataset and minimize the impact of comment preprocessing. Thirdly, it analyzes the performance of pre-trained and fine-tuned models on the Buggilla dataset in a zero-shot and self-supervised setting. Fourthly, the study presents F1-score, F2-score, and the varplot metric to evaluate the models' performance in different scenarios. Lastly, the research finds that fine-tuning strategies have a

In a network with multiple relay nodes, collaborative transmission can extend the reach of a base station's wireless coverage, but it also requires a predetermined scheduling of relay nodes and power allocation to ensure a seamless connection. Since power usage varies significantly with transmission distance, finding an efficient power distribution schedule to maximize energy savings while maintaining coverage is a critical challenge. To address this issue, we introduce a practical solution called Integrated Relay Scheduling and Power Allocation (IRSPA) that involves a two-stage encoding method. The first stage encodes data using a conventional method, but when a base station and relay share a frequency band, it undergoes a secondary encoding at the base station before transmission. As there's no interference from other nodes, this secondary encoding can transfer maximum information while maintaining a stable connection, thus contributing to a significant reduction in overall network power consumption. We analyze the method's efficiency from a collaborative network information theory perspective and observe that the resulting power distribution schedule achieves a higher throughput and minimizes power consumption compared to other scheduling methods. Simulation results confirm our theoretical findings, demonstrating that our proposed scheme leads to a 23% reduction in power consumption compared to a timed-rotating scheduling approach.

To develop a new theoretical approach, we've incorporated the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states into a relativistic version of the initial principles theory, incorporating density functional theory. By integrating the Klein factors from the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states into the surface Green function, we've determined that the spin polarization of the local moment is not significantly influenced by a spin-orbit coupling effect. Additionally, we've discovered that the character of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states changes depending on the type of magnetic impurity. Furthermore, considering the relativistic effects, an Mn dimmer is more likely to form a double magnetic moment, as opposed to the non-relativistic prediction of a single moment.

Recent advancements in ADRK have led to faster alignment of distribution shifts by training GANs using real-time data. Yet, since GANs aren't optimized for diversity, they often cause significant prejudice in resulting data. Our solution involves using DNN filters, which use dynamics to evaluate generated samples and select those that best fit target distributions. We test our approach on adversarial pre-trained models against baseline methods, seeing significant reduction in prejudice and better alignment results for data sequences. Furthermore, our findings also highlight the benefits of specific network architecture designs in adapting to changing distribution shifts.

Satellite images cover vast areas, typically in high resolution, revealing distinct edge patterns associated with essential features like bridges, trees, buildings, and roads. Identifying these edges enables the extraction of information about terrain, architecture, and transportation systems. Although convolutional neural networks deliver outstanding edge detection results, they necessitate substantial computational resources, prompt high bandwidth data transfer, and involve intricate programming. Some applications of satellite imaging are improved by utilizing detailed information related to edges detected by these neural networks. Nevertheless, there is also great advantage in systems that only identify large-scale edges, especially in applications such as the detection of very large-scale structures (e.g., forests, step farms, etc.). Therefore, there is a demand for a system that can simultaneously process large images and derive large-scale edge information without being dependent on neural networks. Our proposed system should be based on the A-Discrete Curve Process, similar to Gerstner, for large-scale edge detection in satellite images. It is built upon the existing MReefs tool and the Discrete Curvature feature and is designed to be highly efficient, especially for large-scale processing of satellite images. Our system is tested on two satellite image datasets: KU Leuven dataset and an image from Google Earth. Our results indicate that the edge information extracted is accurate and relevant, especially focusing on large-scale features. Furthermore, our system is capable of processing and analyzing satellite images quickly and efficiently, even on large scales.

The analysis of high-intensity x-ray absorption spectra benefits from the electron group concept. Typically, this matter is discussed in relation to specific bound states or unbound continua. Research on the dynamics of x-ray absorption has been primarily conducted using one-particle or two-particle models. By incorporating the electron group framework, we can simplify these models and develop a rate equation for interacting multi-electron groups as a unified, single-particle approach. At a fundamental level, this framework can be applied to charge fluctuations in metals and the analysis of high-intensity x-ray absorption, such as in the case of nitrogen in a metal like tungsten. This approach allows for the separation of excitations into metal and nitrogen sub-systems, accurately describing the initial process of nitrogen's p-orbital excitation and later relaxing according to a specific decay rate.

Our research introduces an innovative architecture for the modulation categorization task that safeguards against the manipulation of generator inputs. The existing problem of existing generators, which can be easily compromised by adversarial inputs. This vulnerability allows a smart discriminator to produce high accuracy even when provided with such inputs. In contrast, our new architecture is immune to manipulation by adversarial inputs which can classify the different types of modulation with high accuracy. The success of this new architecture is measured based on the distance between the means of two probability distributions. The probability distributions are calculated based on the output values from the model's last layer for a specific type of modulation. The difference in probability distributions is considered as a form of distance between the two types of modulation in the modulation space. The following are the key findings of our work: (1) a novel model architecture, called the blend generator, is introduced which is able to maintain balance between the types of modulation signals during training, (2) the potential of the blend generator has been confirmed through its performance using real world signals, (3) the model has been further validated by assessing its performance in scenarios where the input signals are compromised, as well as by its performance within the modulation classification task. The models' performance is evaluated using three distinct metrics: (a) the variation of the modulation base signal; (b) the variation of noise injected into the modulation base signal; and (c) the variation of combined signal consisting of modulation base signal and injected noise.

Utilizing deep learning to automate multiple sclerosis segmentation for large-scale research purposes remains challenging due to limited access to diverse, large-scale datasets. Most current methods are trained on a single dataset and then directly applied to a task of segmenting a different dataset, which is known as a domain shift. However, this approach has its limitations because it fails to account for potential variations in datasets. Previous studies show that continuous learning methods, which update models incrementally as new data arrives, can effectively deal with domain shifts. Despite their potential, these methods often require access to a series of datasets and can suffer from data accumulation problems. This study simulates real-world settings by training multiple sclerosis segmentation models successively on consecutive datasets of increasing difficulty and evaluates them against a baseline method that is trained from scratch with no access to previously used datasets. Our results show that continuous learning methods outperform the baseline method across all settings. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on a simple data augmentation strategy that mitigates domain shifts. This indicates that a more effective strategy is required to handle domain shifts in multiple sclerosis segmentation tasks.

The contrast sensitivity of digital images is a vital factor that distinguishes it from physical artwork. Contrast enhances images by means of spatial variations between light and dark areas, which can be achieved through high-contrast elements as well as detailed textures and patterns. This process is notably effective in image types such as line art and halftones, which rely heavily on contrast for visual representation. Despite the significance of contrast, previous methods of image processing and enhancement have largely neglected its value, focusing instead on measures like brightness and color balance. This study seeks to understand the impact of contrast on digital images, develop a method for measuring contrast, and automate the identification and correction of images that require contrast enhancement. Our proposed algorithm effectively increases the contrast of images like line art and halftones, which would otherwise be compromised by existing processing methods.

General models of intelligent systems require a representation of their environment that decreases uncertainty over time as the models accumulate experience. Existing structures for uncertainty in statistical learning theories are rooted in the principles of information theory, but existing models often fail to account for the specific challenges posed by complex systems that exhibit non-reversible or time-dependent behavior. In contrast, we propose a novel uncertainty structure for the dynamical challenges posed by these complex systems, and we demonstrate its practical application to a model of a dc microelectromechanical device that exhibits non-reversible charge dynamics.

We have discovered through VVV Survey observations that a massive dark nebula, known as the Dragon infrared dark nebula, is exhibiting characteristics of expanding gas-rich systems, similar to those found in the Rosette Nebula, due to the influx of gas. Our findings show molecular gas surrounding this nebula and a notable increase in 24 $\mu$m dust temperature, indicating the presence of stellar energy source(s). Based on the appearance of curved and elevated ridges in the $^{12}$CO(1-0) intensity maps, it is deduced that the Dragon nebula is undergoing radial expansion. This transformation is thought to be a result of the compression of gas by newly formed or emerging massive stars, possibly along a pre-existing dust pillar, as a result of dynamical influence or common envelope interaction. Estimates suggest a total mass of approximately 8.6 x 10$^{4}$ M$_{\odot}$ for the surrounding gas, indicating the gas surrounding the Dragon nebula is significantly less massive than that of the Rosette Nebula. This substantial mass disparity presents an intriguing challenge, as it contrasts with the typical outcome typically observed in star-forming molecular clouds, where gas mass far exceeds that of dust. This exceptional circumstance raises the possibility that gas-rich regions, akin to the Dragon nebula, may play a crucial role in the formation of massive stars through the incorporation of gas. If this theory holds true, it could potentially explain the exceptional rarity of gas-rich regions, as

High-resolution simulations of Primordial Black Hole (PBH) shadows are achievable with modern computational capabilities, and can be initiated using PBH masses drawn from N-body simulations of structure formation.  A new, publicly available code called PopSyCLE allows for the precise calculation of PBH mass functions and properties.  This code is used to generate PBH shadows in a series of cosmic environments with varying levels of resolution.  A study of PBH shadows formed in these simulations reveals that PBH dark matter contributions can significantly impact observations in strong gravitational fields.  Notably, low-mass PBHs have a major influence on observations of PBH shadows produced in certain cosmic environments.  This effect, however, can be diminished in simulations modeling the formation of massive galaxy clusters.  Further research may use these simulations to assess how PBH shadows interact with surrounding environments and develop a more comprehensive understanding of PBH physics.

A number of scientific research areas that incorporate complex particles benefit from understanding low-friction conditions.  A specific system consisting of interacting wedges, formed by two spheres in three-dimensional space, was found to exhibit unique behavior when subjected to external forces in an infinite environment. This system displays varying phases, which arise due to the splay order's restrictions, and it has been thoroughly analyzed using graphical representations of the necessary conditions for these phases. As a key phase transitions occur when the opposing walls of the wedge touch spheres, a distinction is made between the splay's effective range, which is either limited to this contact to the farthest point from it. A detailed overview of these phases, which categorize based on the splay's range, is provided in the classification process. Additionally, the most probable splay profiles for each phase have been graphically depicted, and it was discovered that the splay's effective range affects the system's interaction between its components. A description of the system's behavior has also been included in the paper.

Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing are largely attributed to the capabilities of large language models. Unique Token Adaptation (UTA) provides an effective way to incorporate external knowledge into these models, enabling the adjustment of parameters without the need for significant modifications. However, the conventional UTA approach leads to the adaptation of numerous parameters, resulting in inefficient use of computation resources and time-consuming training processes. To mitigate these issues, we present a novel method, Parameter-Efficient Adjustment, to refine language models by assigning importance scores to model components and selectively updating parameters during the adaptation process. Our experiments with multiple models and scenarios demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, yielding consistent improvements in performance and significant reductions in training time and the number of adjusted parameters.

The SET augmentation (SEA) problem, a subset choice problem in the field of multi-objective optimization, has been gaining attention from scholars due to the diverse applications of set theory. In contrast to conventional subset choice problems, which often involve a limited number of choices, SEA characterizes a desirability function with an exponentially large number of possible outcomes. Our research centers on an algorithm called the Contextual Linear List-Valued Preference Ranking-considering Augmentation Costs-according to Priorities (CLLARP-c), which makes preferences explicit through a context-specific desirability function. Our results, derived from a Bayesian network setting, show that, under certain conditions, CLLARP-c achieves a 63% improvement in solution quality over its non-contextual counterpart, with an exponential decrease in computation time. Furthermore, our simulations demonstrate that CLLARP-c outperforms other competing algorithms in various set theory applications.

Observations of temperature-induced changes in structural and dynamic properties in polymer liquids suggest a connection between thermodynamics and dynamics.  To investigate this relationship, we used simulations to measure volume and mean square bond length fluctuations in polycarbonate liquids and found that dynamic property shifts correlate with thermodynamic property changes in line with a widely accepted relationship for physical systems.  This result indicates a link between thermodynamics and dynamics in these glass-forming liquids.  Moreover, the findings show that dynamic property shifts can serve as an indicator of approaching a glass state and inform our understanding of relaxation mechanisms in polymer liquids.

Our study delves into the effectiveness of cutting-edge Transformer models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, in handling rejection candidates during real-time speech recognition. By incorporating a rejection criterion based on uncertainty metrics, low-confidence outputs can be promptly filtered out, significantly enhancing overall speech recognition performance. To achieve this effectively, we must understand how models process rejection candidates and can be forced to produce them. Consequently, we propose a novel training approach inspired by how children learn from their mistakes, involving both generative and discriminative techniques that leverage rejection candidates. This methodology proves to be highly effective in producing rejection candidates on various benchmark datasets, with our research covering two prominent datasets: Librispeech and RedDialect.

The underlying assumption of most AI models is that their input conditions are fixed and unchanging. However, this assumption contradicts the fundamental principle of human creativity, which relies on a dynamic interplay between past experiences, present awareness, and anticipated outcomes. To address this discrepancy, we're exploring a novel approach that enables machines to anticipate and utilize future information, drawing from both intrinsic and extrinsic sources. By incorporating long-term motivations and goal-oriented systems, we're enabling machines to seamlessly integrate creativity and goal-oriented learning. Through a series of systematic evaluations, we're demonstrating that our proposed method significantly enhances creative output in both open-ended and constrained generation tasks, surpassing existing standards.

This study calculates the Kontsevich weights for specific graph configurations - relation and curvature graphs in symplectic Poisson systems. These graph representations simplify the visualization of relations between variables and their correlations in symplectic Poisson structures, which can be utilized to represent symplectic manifolds as well as their transformations under evolution processes. The derived formulas provide a direct computational approach to determine the curvature graph weights, offering a potential alternative to previously established methods in symplectic field theories.

We analyze the dynamics of two-interactting scalar fields in a conformal field theory framework, with a specific large-N limit. By integrating the fields into an AdS space, we generate a dynamics that is encoded in a 4D bulk theory describing interacting scalar fields. Through this approach, we can explore the effect of different couplings on the properties of the scalar fields. By integrating the fields into an AdS space, we can explore the properties of the scalar fields at high temperature and information entropy within the 3D half-space. Our analysis reveals that thermal behavior differs significantly from information entropy, with the latter exhibiting more intricate couplings. For certain couplings, our analysis predicts a thermal phase transition. Notably, our findings demonstrate that thermal behavior can arise from entanglement, even in the absence of thermal fluctuations.

We address specific numerical inaccuracies and logical errors in the authors' previous paper, uncovering a deeper issue arising from a finite basis for the space of continuous positive functions on the state space of a Markov process. This fundamental concern renders numerous theorems within Chapter 7, Chapter 8, and Chapter 9 invalid.

Recent studies using the Fermi Large Area Telescope have revealed an unusual and widespread gamma-ray emission in the sky that is not correlated with known galaxies or their environments. This gamma-ray signal, dubbed the "Gamma-Galaxy X-ray Clump (GXC)" phenomenon, is observed near superclusters of galaxies and is characterized by a power-law spectrum with a high photon index. Previous research found that the gamma-ray energy distribution of these GXCs resembles that of accelerated primary cosmic rays, indicating a non-thermal origin. Notably, the gamma-ray signal associated with superclusters of galaxies is significantly brighter than the sum of the contributions from their constituent groups and clusters, suggesting a third component of non-thermal emission separate from intra-group/cluster and background signals. These findings suggest that the GXC phenomenon may be a novel and widespread astrophysical phenomenon, representing a novel "third component" apart from thermal galaxy clusters and non-thermal cosmic rays.

We investigate the phenomenon of cosmological collider physics using quantum fluctuations in the universe's gravitational field. These fluctuations emerge due to the nonlinear dynamics of the gravitational field and can be utilized to gather insights into the initial conditions of the universe. By examining the one-particle and two-particle scattering behaviors, we find that non-linear fluctuations produce local features in the gravitational field, characterized by specific symmetry breaking and scale properties, which are rooted in the initial state of the universe. Notably, the spatial arrangement of these features corresponds directly to the trajectories of massive particles.

This study aims to investigate the ability of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to differentiate between the semantic meaning and visual appearance of similar images. It has been observed that these networks, being opaque, provide little insight into the image features that they use for classification purposes. By applying a novel filter visualization technique that focuses on the subtle differences between image pairs with distinct meanings but similar visual content, we have gained a deeper understanding of the image features that CNNs have learned during the training process. These localized explanations, which can be applied to a wide range of natural language tasks, provide a crucial framework for evaluating the transparency of deep learning models. Moreover, the fact that these explanations can be interpreted both visually and linguistically enhances their utility as a complementary framework for analyzing CNN performance from a human-centric perspective.

Using a long-range elastic interaction model, we study the effects of geometric constraints and phonon interactions on the attraction experienced between charged defects in one-dimensional cuprate systems. Our research demonstrates that in these systems, the primary contribution to attraction comes from phonon interactions rather than the inherent properties of the materials. Furthermore, by analyzing the properties of paired defect states, we find that the polarization of the material increases without bound as the inter-defect distance decreases, a phenomenon characterized by an attractive potential that behaves like a 2D system at short ranges. This phenomenon is ultimately driven by the coupling of phonons to the electric field, producing an unconventional, unexplored phenomenon in the field of physics.

To safeguard our personal data, regulating access to it is essential.
Authorizations manage how we can use this data, and while current approaches
are static, certain situations demand dynamic handling.  A person's
medical history contains subtle hints about their future well-being and health,
and using these hints along with authorized actions requires a causal
learning method to predict future outcomes accurately.
We propose an algorithm that assesses available data to determine cause-and-effect relationships and, based on this analysis, suggests possible actions to take in order to achieve a desired result.
This method then learns to predict various scenarios based on the learned relationships and the impact of different choices.
Using the French medical database PDMH, we tested our approach, aiming to make predictions about a person's quality of life; the results indicate that taking certain actions has a significant impact on this prediction, and our approach outperforms other methods in this task.

The stability of the magnetization structure in a specific chiral magnet, Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, has been examined when subjected to external fields. Through the utilization of micromagnetic simulations, it was discovered that a specific type of particle at zero temperature exhibits enhanced stability when compared to another, when the micromagnetic energy equations are converted into topological constraints. This finding reveals the connection between magnetization stability and the topology of the system's phase space, demonstrating that stable configurations are embedded within an isolated island. Additionally, it was observed that, at higher temperatures, the system can transition into a state with uniformly tilted magnetization, resulting in a series of interconnected islands of metastability. A comprehensive study of the system's phase diagram provides insight into the underlying physical processes that cause this behavior, ultimately establishing a model that can guide the design of particle configurations in other similar systems.

We will examine specific estimators in high-dimensional time series frameworks, specifically focusing on the high-dimensional dynamic influence model and its variants. A HDIM is a type of vector autoregression model where each element of a vector has a unique, potentially complex effect on other elements within the vector, both in the past and present. Our discussion will center on the dynamic influence of one variable on another across different models, highlighting non-convex optimization techniques and theoretical justification, as well as drawing connections to other areas of study. A hydraulic equilibrium model will also be explored as an example of models that expand upon the HDIM framework, offering potential avenues of future research.

The Point Static Method is a straightforward technique that helps address the balance issue in nonlinear programming by converting an unevenly balanced system into a solvable form. Its basic concept is founded on the dynamic point method, which iteratively constructs a Kuhn-Tucker multiplier for each constraint, making the initial balance issue resolvable. The Point Static Method further simplifies this process by eliminating the need for iterative calculations, thereby achieving the same goal as the dynamic point method through a more efficient approach. As a result, any dynamic point method can be used in conjunction with Point Static to ensure convergence. Furthermore, this method has been successfully tested on a transcritical optimal control problem with multipoint boundary conditions and in a complete sufficient transversality condition for a state-constrained optimal control problem.

A novel machine learning-based method, named Bayesian Neural Networks for U reversible Steganography (BNN-US), has been developed to accurately predict the original cover image given a watermarked image. BNN-US utilizes a multi-layered neural network with a Bayesian framework, which approximates the conditional probability of the cover image given the watermark and the ground truth. Through empirical testing, BNN-US has demonstrated superior performance to state-of-the-art alternatives in generating high-quality steganographic images for popular images.

The dynamic processes within the Earth's core and younger/older geomagnetic bodies remain poorly understood, with various theories existing about their origin. The current research models how heat and energy interact in a global core to produce a magnetic field, taking into account the movement of fluids and the effects it has on the field's structure. The simulated results suggest a connection between the energy of turbulent motion and the generation of the magnetic field, with its behavior influenced by the way this energy changes depending on the scale. To produce a realistic model, it's necessary to use a comprehensive approach that incorporates all the effects of turbulent motion, rather than making assumptions about its properties. This research finds that without a specific type of movement, thermal influences can't effectively generate the magnetic field on their own. The simulated results show that as the movement of fluids changes speed and direction, the type of magnetic field it generates changes from simple to complex shapes, with possible implications for our understanding of the process that creates magnetic fields in the Earth's core.

Recent observations at the ALMA revealed a massive molecular explosion in the galactic center of NGC4945, a highly inclined spiral galaxy, which was discovered following a sudden increase in its 12mm continuum radiation by a factor of 3. The explosion, equivalent to the mass of 380 years' worth of typical stellar formation in our galaxy, was concentrated in 17 pixels and comprised 40 million times the mass of our sun in gas and dust. Analysis of the radiation and gas velocities suggest this event was caused by a cloud of hot dust and gas that was ejected at 300 kilometers per second, which was positioned at the center of the galaxy, directly below a massive baryonic star. This event is believed to be the first visual proof of a'molecular eruption', a phenomenon previously hypothesized to be possible in galaxies with high infrared radiation. Due to its similarity to star-forming explosions, this event may offer valuable insights into the most intense phenomena of our universe, which could be observed in galaxies with high infrared radiation.

A new finite element method was developed for the quasilinear diffusion equation, which governs electron heating in magnetized plasmas during microinstabilities. The approach exploits symmetry properties in the coefficient matrix and implements conservative numerical techniques based on a mixed finite element method, resulting in robust and accurate solutions. The method achieves unconditional stability and is characterized by optimal convergence rates, which were validated through a series of numerical experiments evaluating its effectiveness and consistency.

The recently introduced SDIMSIM algorithm offers a straightforward approach to solving certain types of differential equations, and we have now modified it to accommodate equations with variable step sizes. Building on the L-stable Runge-Kutta Galerkin method, we developed this approach and tested it on a few notable models, including the logistic equation, the Lotka-Volterra model, and the predator-prey model. Our simulations demonstrate that this new method maintains accuracy and stability for a wide range of step size values, outperforming traditional methods in some cases.

This study investigates the exponential stability of abelian c0-semigroups within a real Banach space, focusing on the relationship between Lyapunov-type inequalities and the robustness of the semigroups. We establish two key criteria: the first involves the uniform boundedness of the semigroup and a specific condition related to the resolvent, while the second considers the robustness of the semigroup directly on the Banach space. Notably, the second criterion provides stronger insights, including the ability to eliminate the requirement of strong differentiability and the presence of an operator bound for the semigroup. Additionally, we constructed a counterexample that demonstrates the inapplicability of certain prior theories.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a Python software program designed to calculate how ground-state muonium interacts with various substances via photon exchange. MuMuPy is used to predict muonium's interaction with substances at their reference points, given specific photon energies. Results are displayed graphically and in table form, including relevant data such as substance mass, energy, radius, coulomb factor, and total cross-sectional area at a particular energy. Additionally, this program determines the likelihood of muonium survival after such interactions. The findings presented involve the potential of muonium to bind with electrons in substances and the effect of dimuonium binding energy on dimuonium's decay rate into photon pairs. All calculations presented in this work adhere to the principles of natural dimensionality and units. Based on these predictions, this study identifies suitable substances for dimuonium physics experiments and explores the possibility of creating'muonium gases' within/substance r$_{0}$ domains.

This research involves evaluating investment strategies and portfolio policies for a solo investor who experiences an abnormal increase in wealth, beyond that of their peers. The study shows that by utilizing a power utility function to measure wealth growth relative to market performance, the abnormal wealth can be maximized. The analysis reveals a straightforward method to customize a portfolio policy that is personal to each investor, taking into consideration the shape of their individual wealth distribution. The findings also show how the properties of the underlying asset distribution affect investment decisions, without assuming a specific, common asset distribution. The study focuses on two types of abnormal wealth: one being a fixed percentage and the other more variable, and shows how each's distinct characteristics influence investment behavior and strategies.

High-resolution 21-cm spectra of 60 galaxies with low masses or isolated environments have been analyzed and interpreted. Ten galaxies in this sample have previously unexamined spectra, while the remaining 50 have had their spectra re-evaluated with higher precision. A particular focus was placed on detecting warm gas with temperatures between 10,000 K and 30,000 K, which is found through absorption of radio signals from Lyman series transitions. It has been discovered that this warm gas consistently exists at early and late stages of galaxy development, as well as across a wide range of galaxy masses. The quantity of warm gas relative to total hydrogen is typically between 0.1 and 0.5 percent, although it occasionally exceeds 1 percent. The temperature of this warm gas tends to increase as the galaxy's metal content increases, while its abundance appears to decrease with increasing distance from the centre of the galaxy's dark matter halo. The necessary metal content for activating warm gas through metal-enrichment is estimated to be around 0.6 times 10 to the power of -3 solar masses per cubic parsec. The warm gas's kinetic energy is typically a small fraction of its thermal energy, suggesting that star-forming galaxies contain little to no kinetically hot intergalactic medium. The relationship between galaxy environment and warm gas abundance is consistent with previous research, as galaxies in denser environments tend to have lower amounts of warm gas.
